Van Morrison – Blowing Your Mind (1967)
Posted on December 25, 2017

Blowin’ Your Mind! is the debut album by Northern Irish musician Van Morrison, released in 1967. It was recorded 28–29 March 1967 and contained his first solo pop hit “Brown Eyed Girl”. It was included by Rolling Stone as one of the 40 Essential Albums of 1967.

Morrison does not regard this record as a true album, as Bert Berns compiled and released it without his consent. A few months previously, Morrison had carelessly signed a contract that he had not fully studied and it stipulated that he would surrender virtually all control of the material he would record with Bang Records. The songs were recorded in March 1967 and had been intended to be released on four separate singles. The album jacket became notorious as a model of bad taste. It featured a strange swirl of circling brown vines (and drug connotation) surrounding a sweaty looking Morrison. Greil Marcus described it as a “monstrously offensive, super psychedelic far out out-of-sight exploding” design. Morrison’s then-wife, Janet Planet, said “He never has been, never will be anything approaching a psychedelic user – wants 
nothing to do with it, wants nothing to do with any drug of any kind”. As the singer recalls, “I got a call saying it was an album coming out and this is the cover. And I saw the cover and I almost threw up, you know.” Later, after Berns’ death, Morrison would express his displeasure on a couple of “nonsense songs” he included on the contractual obligation recording session. One was entitled “Blow in Your Nose,” and another was titled “Nose in Your Blow.”

Of the eight songs on the album, all were composed by Morrison except “Goodbye Baby (Baby Goodbye)” and the last song, “Midnight Special”. Clinton Heylin contends that the first side of the album “makes for one of the great single-sided albums in rock”, whereas Greil Marcus, the album’s most hostile critic, found it “painfully boring, made up of three sweet minutes of ‘Brown Eyed Girl’ and… the sprawling, sensation-dulling ‘T.B. Sheets'”.[8] “He Ain’t Give You None” is an urban tale of “lust, jealousy and sexual disgust.” It references Notting Hill Gate and Curzon Street in London, England, places Morrison would have been familiar with when he lived there during his earlier touring days. It contains the words, “You can leave now if you don’t like what is happening.” Brian Hinton compares “the delighted contempt of the singer, the song’s graveyard pace, the stately organ and stinging guitar” to the Highway 61 period of Bob Dylan.

Entertainment Weekly gave it a B-rating, noting that it “displays the pitfalls of late-’60s blues rock: meandering solos, hippie sentiments, and the occasional fuzz-tone guitar. But 
in the hand of Van the Man, those vices are virtues, and what could have been tedious is often hypnotic.” (by wikipedia)

Although Van Morrison’s first solo album is remembered for containing the immortal pop hit “Brown Eyed Girl,” Blowin’ Your Mind! is actually a dry run for his masterpiece, Astral Weeks. Songs like “Who Drove the Red Sports Car” look to that song cycle, even as “Midnight Special” nods to Morrison’s R&B past. But it’s the agonizing “T.B. Sheets” — all nine-plus minutes of it — that dominates this record and belies its trendy title and pop association. “T.B. Sheets” takes the blues and reinvents it as noble tragedy and humiliating mortality. It’s where Van Morrison emerges as an artist. (by William Ruhlmann)

CATEGORY ARCHIVES: MORRISON VAN
Various Artists – Jools Holland’s Big Band Rhythm & Blues (2001)
Posted on December 3, 2023
1

Julian Miles Holland OBE DL (born 24 January 1958) is an English pianist, bandleader, singer, composer and television presenter. He was an original member of the band Squeeze and has worked with many artists including Marc Almond, Joss Stone, Jayne County, Sting, Eric Clapton, Mark Knopfler, George Harrison, David Gilmour, Ringo Starr and Bono.

From 1982 until 1987, he co-presented the Channel 4 music programme The Tube. Since 1992, he has hosted Later… with Jools Holland, a music-based show aired on BBC2, on which his annual show Hootenanny is based. Holland is a published author and appears on television shows besides his own. He regularly hosted the programme Jools Holland on BBC Radio 2. In 2004 he collaborated with Tom Jones on an album of traditional R&B music.

Holland was born on 24 January 1958 in Blackheath, South East London. At the age of eight, he could play the piano fluently by ear. By his early teens he was appearing regularly in many of the pubs in South East London and the East End Docks.

Holland was educated at Shooters Hill Grammar School in southeast London, from which he was expelled for damaging a teacher’s Triumph Herald.

Holland began his career as a session musician. His first studio session was with Wayne County & the Electric Chairs in 1976 on their track “Fuck Off”

Holland was a founding member of the British pop band Squeeze, formed in March 1974, in which he played keyboards until 1980, through its first three albums, the eponymous Squeeze, Cool for Cats and Argybargy, before pursuing his solo career.

Holland began issuing solo records in 1978, his first EP being Boogie Woogie ’78. He continued his solo career through the early 1980s, releasing an album and several singles between 1981 and 1984. He branched out into TV, co-presenting the Newcastle-based TV music show The Tube with Paula Yates. Holland used the phrase, “be there, or be an ungroovy fucker” in one early evening TV trailer for the show, live across two channels, causing him to be suspended from the show for six weeks. He referred to this in his sitcom The Groovy Fellers with Rowland Rivron. Holland also appeared as a guest host on MTV.

In 1983, Holland played an extended piano solo on The The’s re-recording of “Uncertain Smile” for the album Soul Mining. In 1985, Squeeze (which had continued in Holland’s absence through to 1982) unexpectedly regrouped including Holland as their keyboard player. Holland remained in the band until 1990, at which point he again departed to resume his solo career as a musician and a TV host.

In 1987, Holland formed the Jools Holland Big Band, which consisted of himself and for the show Gilson Lavis from Squeeze, which gradually grew and was renamed as Jools Holland’s Rhythm and Blues Orchestra. In May 2022, it was a 17-piece orchestra and included singers Louise Marshall, Ruby Turner and Holland’s daughter Mabel Ray, as well as his younger brother, singer-songwriter and keyboard player, Christopher Holland.

Between 1988 and 1990 Holland performed and co-hosted along with David Sanborn during the two seasons of the music performance programme Sunday Night on NBC late-night television. Since 1992, he has presented the music programme Later… with Jools Holland, plus an annual New Year’s Eve Hootenanny.

In 1996, Holland signed a recording contract with Warner Bros. Records,[4] and his records are now marketed through Rhino Records.

On 29 November 2002, Holland was in the ensemble of musicians who performed at the Concert for George, which celebrated the music of George Harrison. In January 2005 Holland and his band performed with Eric Clapton as the headline act of the Tsunami Relief Cardiff.[citation needed]

On BBC Radio 2 Holland regularly hosted the programme Jools Holland, a mix of live and recorded music and general chat, featuring studio guests, along with members of his orchestra.

In March 2023, Jimmy Barnes announced the formation of supergroup The Barnestormers, featuring Barnes, Chris Cheney, Slim Jim Phantom, Jools Holland and Kevin Shirley. A self-titled album was released on 26 May 2023

Although credited to Jools Holland, according to Allmusic the album is more of a collection of different songs with different singers, with Holland’s band acting as a kind of “house band” including Eric Clapton, Steve Winwood, Van Morrison and George Harrison. The song “Horse to the Water”, which Harrison wrote with his son Dhani, is the last song recorded before Harrison’s death in 2001 and is therefore his legacy. Jools Holland was able to use the contacts he made as host of the BBC programme Later with Jools Holland for the line-up. The singers range from musical veterans such as Van Morrison and Steve Winwood to representatives of the younger generation such as Jamiroquai and Joe Strummer, a founding member of The Clash.

In addition to the majority of blues and rhythm and blues titles, other styles are also among the songs chosen, such as the ska title “Oranges and Lemons Again” with Suggs or the title “Valentine Moon” with Sam Brown. In addition to cover versions, such as “I Put a Spell on You”, there are songs that were created especially for the album (“The Return of the Blues Cowboy”, “The Hand That Changed It’s Mind”).

The album reached number 19 in the Billboard Heatseekers Charts (wikipedia)

The world of pop music is very much part of show business, and as such, there as much a culture of stars and celebrities as there is in the movies or television. And for generations, recordings have billed themselves on their star power — combining two or more musical celebrities on one song or album. More of than not, the musical combination is one undertaken with the market in mind, rather than real musical collaboration. But there are exceptions, and I think this week’s CD qualifies as an interesting, and indeed very ambitious venture into combining a remarkable number of well-known musical artists in a single recording, in a record that is also a lot of fun to listen to. It’s the newest CD by veteran British keyboard man Jools Holland, called Jools Holland’s Big Band Rhythm & Blues, and it has guest appearances by not less than 22 different significant, mostly British, musical figures, including Eric Clapton, Steve Winwood, Van Morrison, Sting, and what is reputed to be the last recording by George Harrison recorded a bit more than a month before his death in November. In addition to the noted guests, the CD lives up to its title with no less than 52 studio musicians also providing accompaniment at various times, including a big band and a string orchestra.

Jools Holland is best-known for his tenure as keyboard player in the British band Squeeze. But since then, he has had a program on the BBC called “Later with Jools Holland” a music show spotlighting various well-known guests, so that provided him with the contacts that eventually led to this CD. He also is a big fan of early rock & roll, R&B and soul, and his own recordings over the years have reflected that. So those two facets were combined on this CD, with the guests doing both original songs and old standards in the style. In some cases, it’s a bit out of character for the guest, such as Sting or Soft Cell’s Marc Almond, but at others, such as for Taj Mahal, Dr. John, and Eric Clapton, it’s a perfect fit. And throughout, there is a spirit of good fun, and that really sets this CD apart from other star-studded records, which usually reduce to lowest-common-denominator light-pop. It’s interesting hearing Van Morrison doing a Louis Armstrong song, or John Cale doing some Vegas style crooning. Obviously, some parts are more successful than others, but the lighthearted nature of the CD, in which a lot of stars are apparently having fun, makes up for any of the less satisfying parts of this very generous, 80-minute CD.

Ever since the 1960s, when the British Blues phenomenon happened, with young English musicians essentially re-packaging and bringing back to American rock audiences the great American art form of the blues, the Brits have had a distinctive approach which has evolved into its own style, but still has designs on the original American recordings. Jools Holland, in his recent releases, shows that dichotomy, with echoes of the British Blues bands, but also a distinctly American retro sound, though like other Brits, he sometimes goes a little too far, with too many horns, guitars cranked up a bit too much, tempos taken a bit too fast, and not enough space in the music — something that is essential in the blues. This CD has the same kind of pumped-up, frenetic sound, and that can make this record wear a bit on the listener at times, especially after the novelty of all the stars on the same CD fades, but Holland does mix the album up stylistically some, and overall, it’s an admirable recording, and would be even if there were not as many big names on it.

Though Holland is a decent vocalist, he defers to his guests most of the time on this CD. He does sing a verse here and there, but for the most part, the guests get to sing the songs, quite of few of which were collaborative compositions between Holland and the respective guest.

The track with Sting opens the CD. It’s the old Willie Dixon blues classic Seventh Son, and it’s interesting hearing the normally sophisticated Sting getting down with the blues, and doing a very respectable job. The track illustrates the kind of big-production sound that dominates the CD.

That is followed by what turns out to be its most poignant track, Horse to the Water, featuring George Harrison, and recorded in October 2001, the month before his death. It’s a song Harrison co-wrote with his son Dhani, and while it has the upbeat sound of the rest of the CD, the cryptic, philosophical lyrics made the piece fascinating. Harrison, considering his declining health at the time, sounds in good form.  The guitar solo is presumably by George.

One of the more unusual choices of guests is Joe Strummer, a founding member of the Clash. His guest slot comes on an original joint composition by Strummer and Holland called The Return of the Blues Cowboy. It’s also the track with the least instrumentation. Despite the some tasteful piano work by Holland, Strummer shows he is not exactly a blues singer.

Dr. John appears on another original joint composition with Holland called The Hand That Changed Its Mind. Holland does the introductory lead vocal, before the Dr. John makes his entrance. Musically, the track perhaps best captures the spirit of jump band blues that for which Holland seems always to be striving.

There are some slower tracks, including an unexpected treatment of Screamin’ Jay Hawkins’ classic I Put a Spell on You, sung by Mica Paris with guitar from Pink Floyd’s David Gilmour. The result quite engaging, though the addition of the string section does go a bit over the top.

Another of the most fascinating combinations is the track featuring Van Morrison, the Louis Armstrong composition, Back o’ Town Blues. The arrangement maintains the spirit of the original music, though like a lot of Holland’s work, the tempo is a little too fast and there are too many horns.

Dire Straits founder Mark Knopfler appears in a straight rockabilly arrangement of his song called Mademoiselle Will Decide. Although Knopfler has explored the edges of this style with Dire Straits, this track works particularly well.

The CD is not without some disappointments. One of my favorite acoustic bluesmen, Eric Bibb, makes an appearance on All That You Are, a song he co-wrote with Holland. The song’s lyrics lend themselves to the kind of intimate arrangements that mark Bibb’s own albums, but the arrangement here is more along the lines of a Phil Spector production, and it just sounds overblown.

Steve Winwood, who got his start in the British Blues days, appears on what is definitely one of the CD’s highlights, I’m Ready, another Willie Dixon song, first recorded by Muddy Waters.

John Cale, who first came to fame as a member of the Velvet Underground, appears on I’ll Be Around an old Johnny Mercer song, done as a kind of Sinatra/Vegas production. It definitely leaves one scratching one’s head wondering if it was serious, or done as high camp. It doesn’t quite work either way.

The CD ventures into some ska on two tracks. One features Jamiroquai doing another Tin Pan Alley standard I’m in the Mood for Love. Despite the interesting concept, the result has a kind of perfunctory sound, never really catching fire.

The final track features Eric Clapton in a soulful performance of Ray Charles’ What Would I Do without You. In this case all the horns and strings work well, and Clapton is in great form.

Even among all-star recordings, Jools Holland’s Big Band Rhythm & Blues is impressive for its roster of special guests, who also include Taj Mahal, Paul Weller, Chris Difford, Holland’s former band-mate in Squeeze, The Stereophonics, and Mick Hucknall. The fact that the music is fun, and generally unpretentious also sets this project apart. About the only drawback is the fact that the CD very much lives up to his title. Often the horn and string sections can be a little overwhelming often to the point of being musically bombastic. Fifty-two backing musicians can be a bit much at times, and the music can have a kind of in-your-face quality than makes one want to take at least one intermission in the course of the hour and twenty minutes of the CD.

That pushy quality also extends to the album’s sonics. The mix is heavily compressed and almost constantly loud, even when the music tries to slow down. Sometimes that results in noticeable distortion on the vocals, and it also contributes to a somewhat fatiguing sound — as interesting as it is, I felt I needed to take a break from listening after a while, especially considering the CD’s length. Some restraint in both the scale of the musical arrangements and the volume of the mix would have helped a great deal.

Even in these days of media-driven celebrity culture, it’s rare to get as many well-known artists on a single CD. But Jools Holland’s Big Band Rhythm and Blues despite a few lapses, is an album that’s both fascinating and a lot of fun. (by George D. Graham.)

Van Morrison – The Best Of Van Morrison (1990)
Posted on January 7, 2022

Sir George Ivan Morrison OBE (born 31 August 1945), known professionally as Van Morrison, is a Northern Irish singer-songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and record producer whose recording career spans seven decades. He has won two Grammy Awards.

Morrison began performing as a teenager in the late 1950s. He played a variety of instruments such as guitar, harmonica, keyboards and saxophone for several Irish showbands, covering the popular hits of that time. Known as “Van the Man” to his fans, Morrison rose to prominence in the mid-1960s as the lead singer of the Northern Irish R&B and rock band Them. With Them, he recorded the garage band classic “Gloria”.

Under the pop-oriented guidance of Bert Berns, Morrison’s solo career began in 1967 with the release of the hit single “Brown Eyed Girl”. After Berns’s death, Warner Bros. Records bought out Morrison’s contract and allowed him three sessions to record Astral Weeks (1968). While initially a poor seller, the album has become regarded as a classic. Moondance (1970) established Morrison as a major artist, and he built on his reputation throughout the 1970s with a series of acclaimed albums and live performances.

Much of Morrison’s music is structured around the conventions of soul music and R&B. An equal part of his catalogue consists of lengthy, spiritually inspired musical journeys that show the influence of Celtic tradition, jazz and stream-of-consciousness narrative, such as the album Astral Weeks The two strains together are sometimes referred to as “Celtic soul”. His live performances have been described as “transcendental” and “inspired”, and his music as attaining “a kind of violent transcendence”.

Morrison’s albums have performed well in Ireland and the UK, with more than 40 reaching the UK top 40. With the release of Latest Record Project, Volume 1 he scored top ten albums in the UK in four consecutive decades. Eighteen of his albums have reached the top 40 in the United States, twelve of them between 1997 and 2017. He has received two Grammy Awards, the 1994 Brit Award for Outstanding Contribution to Music, the 2017 Americana Music Lifetime Achievement Award for Songwriting and has been inducted into both the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame. In 2016, he was knighted for services to the music industry and to tourism in Northern Ireland.

The Best of Van Morrison is a compilation album by Northern Irish singer-songwriter Van Morrison. It compiles songs spanning 25 years of his recording career. Released in 1990 by Polydor Records, the album was a critical and commercial success, becoming one of the best-selling records of the 1990s and helping revive Morrison’s mainstream popularity. Its success encouraged him to release a second and third greatest hits volume in 1993 and 2007, respectively. The album remains Morrison’s best-seller.

The Best of Van Morrison was Morrison’s first greatest hits album and featured songs that were compiled from 25 years of material. including “Wonderful Remark”, a song which first appeared on the soundtrack to the 1983 film The King of Comedy. The album became one of the best-selling records of the 1990s, spending a year and a half on the UK charts, helping Morrison regain his commercial popularity during the decade. It also debuted at number one in Australia on the ARIA Albums Chart. In the United States, the album never reached the Top 40 of the Billboard 200 but remained on the chart for more than four-and-a-half years. In 2002, the album was certified quadruple platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), having shipped four million copies in the US. Morrison was reluctant at first to have a greatest hits album released, although its success encouraged him to personally select tracks for the second and third volumes in 1993 and 2007, respectively. “As the story goes, Van Morrison wanted nothing to do with his first greatest hits collection”, wrote Andrew Gilstrap from PopMatters. “He probably warmed up to the idea, though, after the sales figures started pouring in—year after year after year.”

The Best of Van Morrison remains his best-selling release.(wikipedia)

For an artist who’s doggedly album-oriented, plus a songwriter who revels in subtlety, Van Morrison doesn’t seem like a logical candidate for a successful greatest-hits compilation. Nevertheless, The Best of Van Morrison is a crackerjack compilation, tracing Van the Man from his days with Them, through his best-known tunes (“Brown-Eyed Girl,” “Moondance,” “Blue Money,” “Wild Night”), to highlights from the ’70s and ’80s cult efforts, topped off by “Wonderful Remark,” a song first heard on the King of Comedy soundtrack. This collection makes Morrison’s work seem a little more immediate and accessible than it usually is, but that’s a blessing, since it provides a great summary of his hits and a nice introduction for the curious. Yes, it could have dug deeper into the catalog, but as a sampler, it can’t be faulted. (by Stephen Thomas Erlewine)

Van Morrison, Lonnie Donegan & Chris Barber – The Skiffle Sessions – Live In Belfast (2000)
Posted on March 25, 2019

The Skiffle Sessions – Live In Belfast 1998 is a live album by Northern Irish singer-songwriter Van Morrison, with Lonnie Donegan and Chris Barber, released in 2000 (see 2000 in music). Lonnie Donegan had played with the Chris Barber Jazz Band when he had his first hit with “Rock Island Line”/”John Henry” in 1955. He had been a childhood influence on Van Morrison, who had first performed in his own skiffle band with schoolmates when he was twelve years old in Belfast, Northern Ireland. This was Donegan’s first album in twenty years, reviving his career until his death in 2002.

Recorded on 20 and 21 November 1998 at Whitla Hall, Belfast, Northern Ireland. In 1977, Morrison had discussed recording an album of skiffle music with Dr. John, “because I started off in a skiffle group and there must be millions of other musicians who also began their careers playing that kind of music…” In preparation for this recording, he went to see Donegan perform and invited him to dinner and after a second meeting they arranged to record the sessions live. Dr. John, who was playing in concert in the city’s Ulster Hall the same evening, arrived toward the end of the recording to play piano on the final few tracks. (by wikipedia)

Van Morrison probably chose to give a pair of skiffle concerts in November, 1998 not because he was nostalgic, but because he has genuine love for this music. At least, that’s the impression The Skiffle Sessions gives. It’s a cheerfully old-fashioned yet curiously fresh album. By skipping “Rock Island Line,” the style’s best-known tune, and emphasizing the music’s foundation in American folk, blues, and jazz, they wind up revitalizing skiffle while paying homage to it. Yes, this may be corny at times, yet it’s a clever, diverse record. They delve into blues, letting Barber have a Dixieland trombone solo on “Frankie and Johnny,” invite Dr. John to play some New Orleans on “Goin’ Home” and “Good Morning Blues,” haul out Jimmie Rodgers’ “Muleskinner Blues” and Leadbelly’s “Goodnight Irene,” paying tribute to both country and folk. Only “Don’t You Rock Me Daddio” fits the clichés of skiffle, and here it’s only one side of a rich, generous collection of roots music.

Some might say that this multifaceted approach to skiffle is revisionism, but it isn’t; skiffle itself was a hybrid, drawing from all sorts of American roots music but given an endearing twist by idealist British musicians, who loved the American myth as much as the music. The Skiffle Sessions captures this love of myth and music, while being a hell of a good listen. Morrison’s career has been idiosyncratic and unpredictable, but nothing has been quite as surprising as this. Really, there’s no reason why a skiffle album released in 2000 should be as irresistible as this, but Morrison, Donegan, and Barber bring such heart and love to this music that it’s hard not to be charmed. (by Stephen Thomas Erlewine)

Van Morrison – Inarticulate Speech Of The Heart (1983)
Posted on January 15, 2019
1

Inarticulate Speech of the Heart is the fourteenth studio album by Northern Irish singer-songwriter Van Morrison, released in 1983. Morrison said he arrived at the title from a Shavian saying: “that idea of communicating with as little articulation as possible, at the same time being emotionally articulate”. As his last album for Warner Bros. Records, he decided to do an album of mostly instrumentals. As he explained in 1984, “Sometimes when I’m playing something, I’m just sort of humming along with it, and that’s got a different vibration than an actual song. So the instrumentals just come from trying to get that form of expression, which is not the same as writing a song.” Although not expanded upon, of note is that a special thanks is given to L. Ron Hubbard in the liner notes. The reissued and remastered version of the album contains alternative takes of “Cry for Home” and “Inarticulate Speech of the Heart No. 2”.

The recording sessions took place in California, Dublin, and a series of marathon sessions at the Town House in London. Morrison played piano, guitar and saxophone on these sessions. Two Irish musicians played on the album (Arty McGlynn and Davy Spillane) and overall the music had a strong Celtic colouring. Four of the songs were instrumentals. (by wikipedia)

Almost a forgotten album, Inarticulate Speech of the Heart takes listeners to the deepest, most inward areas of Van Morrison’s renegade Irish soul, the culmination of his spiritual jazz period and also — perhaps not coincidentally — the last record he made for Warner Bros. Four of the 11 tracks are moody instrumentals, which might partly explain the indifference of many rock critics toward the album, although the album’s very title gives a clue to their presence. The mood is predominantly mellow but never flaccid or complacent; there is a radiance that glows throughout. “Higher Than the World” is simply one of the most beautiful recordings Morrison ever made, with Mark Isham’s choir-like synthesizer laying down the lovely backdrop. The instrumental “Connswater” is the most Irish-flavored piece that Morrison had made up to that point, and would continue to be until he recorded with the Chieftains in 1988. “Rave on, John Donne” — in part a recitation invoking a roster of writers over a supple two-chord vamp — seems to have had the longest afterlife, reappearing in Morrison’s live shows and greatest-hits compilations. “The Street Only Knew Your Name” is the only piece that could be classified as a rocker, tempered even here by the synthesizer overlays. The record sold poorly, but many of those who bought it consider it one of the most cherished items in their Van Morrison collections. (by Richard S. Ginell)

Van Morrison – Blowing Your Mind (1967)
Posted on December 25, 2017

Blowin’ Your Mind! is the debut album by Northern Irish musician Van Morrison, released in 1967. It was recorded 28–29 March 1967 and contained his first solo pop hit “Brown Eyed Girl”. It was included by Rolling Stone as one of the 40 Essential Albums of 1967.

Morrison does not regard this record as a true album, as Bert Berns compiled and released it without his consent. A few months previously, Morrison had carelessly signed a contract that he had not fully studied and it stipulated that he would surrender virtually all control of the material he would record with Bang Records. The songs were recorded in March 1967 and had been intended to be released on four separate singles. The album jacket became notorious as a model of bad taste. It featured a strange swirl of circling brown vines (and drug connotation) surrounding a sweaty looking Morrison. Greil Marcus described it as a “monstrously offensive, super psychedelic far out out-of-sight exploding” design. Morrison’s then-wife, Janet Planet, said “He never has been, never will be anything approaching a psychedelic user – wants 
nothing to do with it, wants nothing to do with any drug of any kind”. As the singer recalls, “I got a call saying it was an album coming out and this is the cover. And I saw the cover and I almost threw up, you know.” Later, after Berns’ death, Morrison would express his displeasure on a couple of “nonsense songs” he included on the contractual obligation recording session. One was entitled “Blow in Your Nose,” and another was titled “Nose in Your Blow.”

Of the eight songs on the album, all were composed by Morrison except “Goodbye Baby (Baby Goodbye)” and the last song, “Midnight Special”. Clinton Heylin contends that the first side of the album “makes for one of the great single-sided albums in rock”, whereas Greil Marcus, the album’s most hostile critic, found it “painfully boring, made up of three sweet minutes of ‘Brown Eyed Girl’ and… the sprawling, sensation-dulling ‘T.B. Sheets'”.[8] “He Ain’t Give You None” is an urban tale of “lust, jealousy and sexual disgust.” It references Notting Hill Gate and Curzon Street in London, England, places Morrison would have been familiar with when he lived there during his earlier touring days. It contains the words, “You can leave now if you don’t like what is happening.” Brian Hinton compares “the delighted contempt of the singer, the song’s graveyard pace, the stately organ and stinging guitar” to the Highway 61 period of Bob Dylan.

Entertainment Weekly gave it a B-rating, noting that it “displays the pitfalls of late-’60s blues rock: meandering solos, hippie sentiments, and the occasional fuzz-tone guitar. But 
in the hand of Van the Man, those vices are virtues, and what could have been tedious is often hypnotic.” (by wikipedia)

Although Van Morrison’s first solo album is remembered for containing the immortal pop hit “Brown Eyed Girl,” Blowin’ Your Mind! is actually a dry run for his masterpiece, Astral Weeks. Songs like “Who Drove the Red Sports Car” look to that song cycle, even as “Midnight Special” nods to Morrison’s R&B past. But it’s the agonizing “T.B. Sheets” — all nine-plus minutes of it — that dominates this record and belies its trendy title and pop association. “T.B. Sheets” takes the blues and reinvents it as noble tragedy and humiliating mortality. It’s where Van Morrison emerges as an artist. (by William Ruhlmann)

[1] Music Fanzine | Jersey Beat — https://www.jerseybeat.com/paulsilver.html
Title: Music Fanzine | Jersey Beat

URL Source: https://www.jerseybeat.com/paulsilver.html

Markdown Content:
![Image 1](https://www.jerseybeat.com/images/jb-top1.jpg)
![Image 2: Jersey Beat Music Fanzine](https://www.jerseybeat.com/images/jb-header1.jpg)
![Image 3](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/paulsilver-banner.jpg)![Image 4](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/silver-lining.jpg) ![Image 5](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/drowns-3.jpg) ## THE DROWNS – Harsh Reality (Pirates Press Records, thedrowns.bandcamp.com) It’s been fascinating following the career of The Drowns. From their 2018 debut, _View from the Bottom_, to today, they’ve evolved their sound, played around with genres, and gotten tighter and tighter. They’ve released excellent street punk records, they’ve toyed with classic rock, they’ve put out super-fun glam, and they’ve record some incredible power pop. On this outing, the band brings us a mix that includes 90's melodic punk, street punk, and more. Guitarist/vocalist Rev writes about half the songs, and he favors the bold street punk and glam sounds. The album opens strongly with one of these, “Always a Bastard,” Rev’s gritty voice shouting the lyrics as the high energy music plays behind him. The guitar lines have a cool, lonesome sound to them, and the rhythm section pounds relentlessly. “Relentless” and “”Let’s Start a Cult” are solid street punk tunes, the former with big sing-along gang vocals in the chorus. One of the most fun and unique Rev tunes is “3rd & Pike,” an upbeat mix of glam and Zydeco music, complete with accordion, but with dark lyrics about broken trust. Another good one is the hard-driving “Vengeance,” which mixes glam, hard rock, and street punk. Andy Wylie’s songs tend to be smoother, more focused on power pop and melodic punk sounds. “Have a Heart” has a cool bounce, with a dark melodic punk vibe. “Hellish Tattoo” and “Strangled Voices,” too, have a solid 90's melodic punk sound, with parts that are dark and parts that are bright and poppy. Andy’s vocals sometimes verge on crooning, too, reminding me a little bit of Josh Caterer’s vocals with The Smoking Popes. Speaking of which, my favorite Andy song of the album has to be “Burn the Page,” which oozes poppy music and crooning vocals, bouncy and bright, but with lyrics about the terrible state of the world today. “Death of the Optimist” sees a bit of Rev’s street punk vibe seeping into Andy’s pop punk tune, particularly in the chorus. Although it’s pretty easy to tell the difference between songs written by Rev or Andy, one thing they all have in common is their unrelenting energy. Every Drowns song comes across as an unstoppable force. The boys from Seattle have another winner on their hands. ![Image 6](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/goodnightnobody.jpg) ## GOODNIGHT NOBODY (Sweet Cheetah Records, goodnightnobody.bandcamp.com) Debut albums are always fun. Discovering new music from new bands you’ve never heard of before can sometimes be like hitting the lottery. Goodnight Nobody is a trio that hails from Vermont and plays edgy, noisy indie that injects mathish moments, emo influence, and a bit of punch into their music, and this is their debut LP. I can hear the grit of dissonance, twisted rhythms, and melodic hooks, sometimes sounding like a descendant of Dischord Revolution Summer bands, sometimes sounding more like a 90's post-hardcore band. The opening track falls into the latter category, with grinding guitars and fuzz-filled bass. Vocals are emphatically shouted as the beat pulses hypnotically, as the band jams. “(We’ve Got the) Receipts” is a strong mix of strident post hardcore chords and emo melodic lines and vocals. “Can vs. Should” is another that features both melodic indie/emo, but also a jamming bridge that goes hard toward a psych aesthetic. But it’s the more East Coast emo-sounding tracks that really get me going. “Aurora” has a mid-80's Soulside sort of sound, but maybe gliding along a little more smoothly. “Rosary” reminds me a bit of some of the music Gauge (originator of the Midwest emo sound) was making in the early 90's, making it another favorite. I’m sure the fact that the band had J Robbins (Jawbox, J Robbins Band, Government Issue) produce this helped inform the sound. This is a pretty solid debut. ![Image 7](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/thegoods.jpg) ## THE GOODS – Goodbye Summertime (Dandy Boy Records, dandyboyrecords.bandcamp.com) Following their debut EP in 2023, Oakland’s power poppers The Goods released their debut full-length, _Don’t Spoil the Fun_, last year. Now they’re back with their sophomore LP, and _Goodbye Summertime_ is just in time for the changing of the seasons. And one thing I notice about this LP, in comparison to their debut, is that the new songs are smoother and less raucous, with injections of folk-pop and psych. They’ve also got lusher arrangements, with a fuller sound, going beyond the simplicity of guitar-driven rock 'n' roll. The songs are still jangly power pop, just with less of an edge. They feel more like 60's and 70's guitar pop than 80's power pop, with hints of British Invasion era sounds, too. I really like the mod feel of the opening track, “Lazy,” and the delicate nature of “Love You More” is lovely. We get folksy tunes, with acoustic guitar in the mix, like the melancholy “Don’t Worry,” and there’s the jangly upbeat “Summer’s Almost Gone,” a song about making the most of the time we have. The Goods’ new LP is a pleasant one, but I wish it had more of the raucous nature of the EP. ![Image 8](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/madtab.jpg) ## MAD TAB – Alas! The Bomb Voyage… (Innanuttshell Reekordingz, innanuttshellreekordingz.com) Without the press materials telling me that Mad Tab is a Southern California band, I knew it just from listening to the record. Their brand of punk rock contains an aggressive mix of speedy hardcore, beachy pop punk, skanking ska punk, and even some dub reggae influenced music. There’s solid musicianship and an urgent feel to these songs, which sound super-tight without sounding slick, and that’s a perfect combination for me. Almost from the start we get high energy tracks like “Animals,” which has a fantastic rapid-fire rhythm, crunchy hardcore instrumentals, and a great pop melody. It’s one of the standout tracks of an album full of great songs. I love the harmonies in “Awake,” another speedy poppy hardcore tune. We get a slower grind alternating with gritty hardcore in the quintessentially SoCal “Vans On My Feet.” And I love “All Live,” a song that’s blisteringly fast and melodic, poppy and fun. There are a number of solid ska punk tunes here, including “Loose Teeth” and “Good Boi,” both of which have a nice rock steady lope. We get a history lesson, of a sort, in “Windrush Empire,” a song about the effort to rebuild London after World War II and the importation of cheap labor from the Caribbean, which led to Two Tone culture in the UK. “The Process” mixes ska punk with a grittier vibe, with parts of the song sounding like it comes from the backyards of East L.A. “Work N Pressure,” on the other hand, is brisker and more reminiscent of Operation Ivy, with a mix of street punk grit and skankin’ beats. And songs like “Don’t Blink” mix aggressive hardcore with smoother ska sounds to make something that theoretically shouldn’t exist, but is an amazing track worthy of Bad Brains. The album closer is a fun acoustic ska punk track, showing the band’s versatility. Mad Tab is a great band and Alas! The Bomb Voyage… is a great listen. ![Image 9](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/smugbrothers5.jpg) ## SMUG BROTHERS – Pinhole to Vortex (Anyway Records, smugbrothers.bandcamp.com) Dayton, Ohio’s indie-power-pop masters are getting to be quite prolific! It was just this past May yhey released their career retrospective LP, _Gravity Is Just a Way to Fall_. And that came on the heels of a pair of LPs in 2025! On this latest album, they’ve evolved a little bit away from their British Invasion influences and more toward a solid indie-rock sound, but still informed by classic power pop, with a relaxed vibe and a polished sound. Guitars jangle confidently and the tempos are easygoing. Multi-part vocal harmonies abound, and the music is pleasant. I like the lush sounds of “Kind Enough to Share,” and the deep driving sound of “Bolt Through the Blackout” is pretty cool. Smug Brothers’ vibe on this album is reminding me of current Guided By Voices sort of stuff. Which makes sense, because they’re both Ohio bands. I like the retro folk-psych aesthetic of “Wake Up (Be Your Own Planet)” and “Speeding By the Way Things Used to Look,” and the little trumpet fanfare flourishes of “Picasso Waltzes” are nice. If I have one bit of constructive criticism for Smug Brothers, it would be that there’s less variety in the sounds on this album than in the past. A little change now and then, plus more dynamic range can make for a more engaging listening experience. ![Image 10](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/topdown.jpg) ## TOPDOWN – The Earth & All Its Pavement (Sweet Cheetah Records/ Diverse Chorus Records /topdowntx.bandcamp.com) Austin band Topdown may have only been around since 2024 but they’ve hit the ground running and are already releasing their sophomore LP. The five-piece band plays a sweet blend of post-hardcore, emo, and melodic hardcore, their songs filled with crunch, broad, smooth melodies, and a contrasting mix of lush romantic and hard-edged gritty vocals. I love the way the album opens, with “Adrenaline.” We get a background whine and a big clanging bass in the foreground for a few bars, and then the whole band comes in with explosive energy, Grace’s lead vocals croon with passion. The contrast of the hard-edged pummeling instrumentals and the gorgeous torch song vocals is something to behold. “Dissonance,” which follows, is a broad striding track with moments of pure romance, and it’s about not knowing how to love properly, according to Grace. Another favorite is “Coping Mechanism,” which sometimes jangles with dreamy indie pop vibes, and other times hits you square in the jaw with a big one-two combination punch. There’s also the lovely “Interlude,” which is the stuff of sweet dreams, coming right before the album closer, “Sentimental,” a song that leans heavily into the smooth 2000's emo sound. Topdown’s big dynamic range and the ease in which they cross-blend genres makes _The Earth & All Its Pavement_ a winner. ![Image 11](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/yammerjaw.jpg) ## YAMMER JAW – Burth (yammerjaw.bandcamp.com) Hailing from the unlikeliest of places, Nashville, Yammer Jaw is about the furthest from country music you can get. The band’s debut mini-LP is filled with post-hardcore rage, angular melodic lines, shifting rhythms, and manic noise. The band calls it an EP, but with nine tracks and 26 minutes, it’s almost a full album. The PR materials reference Fugazi and Drive Like Jehu as “For Fans Of” bands. I disagree. Yammer Jaw has more of a Quicksand or Refused intensity, with metallic power and frenzy mixed with the manic anxiety of New York’s Alice Donut. Strong points include the expertly rumbling bass, the unpredictable nature of the songs, and the frenetic intensity of it all. It’s an unending sonic assault that will have you jumping and shouting, and your neighbors banging on the walls. Peak Yammer Jaw can be found in “Apex Creditor,” a track that has a great pun for a title, tons of menace, and lots of shifting vibes. “Gun” has some cool gliding moments amidst the chaos, while “Lamp of Freedom” is the most experimental track, less of a song and more meandering noise plus damning sermon. There’s a lot of political commentary in this album, too, such as in the track, “Sheep,” which likens the population to the titular animal, people spending all their time doomscrolling and following the herd. “It’s seven o’clock, do you know where your freedom is?” the track asks. I think we could have done without “Beefy Streams,” though, which is nothing more than 30 seconds of men peeing into a toilet. But other than that, this is a big muscular debut. * * * ![Image 12](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/bethcameron.jpg) ## BETH CAMERON – The World. Oh No. (Submissive Grin, bethcameronmusic.bandcamp.com) Beth Cameron is, apparently, a big deal in the local Nashville indie music scene. It’s a scene that’s, sadly, overshadowed by the country music industry and doesn’t get the recognition it deserves. I can vouch for that, because I was unfamiliar with Cameron, though this has, thankfully, been corrected. She’s played in various bands, including Forget Cassettes and Black Bra, but The World, Oh No. is her solo debut. The best way I can describe the music on this album is experimental pop music. The songs are mysterious and morose, and they range from subdued to grand. These songs are more aptly described as sonic artwork, with varied textures and tones. There is much darkness and sadness, the instrumentals filled with an undercurrent of noise and whispers, and Cameron’s vocals are pure beauty. After the short introductory “Prodrome,” which introduces an eerie theme that recurs at the end of the album, “Something in the Offing” feels tentative and apprehensive. Piano and drums provide a dirge-like atmosphere, as Cameron’s angelic voice trembles with unease. “Lemonsqueezer,” which follows, reminds me of Laurie Anderson’s performance art music, alternating between spoken word and smooth singing, but the lyrics are dark and devastating. The celestial singing at the end is in stark contrast to the lyrics about a woman who has suffered horribly from abuse, lived with suicidal ideations, and self-medicated to dull the pain. Another standout is “Sympathetic Symphony,” a song with the sound of dystopian science fiction. It’s noisy and dark, with an emphatic rhythm. Halfway through the track, the question comes, “Are you okay?” and the floodgates are opened with loud uncontrolled sobbing. The album’s lead single “HeLa” is huge and bold spacy progressive art rock, reminiscent of Pink Floyd. It tells the true story of a woman, HeLa (Henrietta Lacks), who died of cervical cancer at age 31 in 1951. Doctors harvested her cancer cells, without her knowledge or consent, and that became the first immortalized cell line in medical science. Her cells have been used in countless studies, fueling vaccines for polio, HPV, and COVID-19, and contributing to HIV/AIDs and cancer research. Her family members didn’t even know about this until the 1970s, and there have been legal settlements over this. She may have died, but she has saved millions of lives. She is eternal and everlasting. I love “RIP, OP,” which begins as a simple lament, complete with electric organ and backing vocal choir, giving it a very spiritual feel. But halfway through the organ is replaced by a piano, and the song takes on the vibe of an off-Broadway stage production. And the closing title track, subtitled “Postdrome,” has a truly post-apocalyptic vibe. The wind howls, an out of tune piano pecks out that introductory melody we heard at the beginning of the record, and then we hear a chorus of voices whispering and crying, “Oh no!” This reaches a frenzy and is suddenly cut, replaced with a high pitched tone, background hiss, and solemn voice intoning, “I thought that you were an anchor in the drift of the world. But, no, there isn’t an anchor anywhere. There isn’t an anchor in the drift of the world. Oh, no. I thought you were. Oh, no. The drift of the world.” It’s the stuff of nightmares. Throughout the nearly hour-long album, we’re taken on a journey and confronted. There are uncomfortable truths here that most would not care to admit. It’s difficult, and compelling. It’s outstanding art.![Image 13](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/gay%20agenda.jpeg) ## THE GAY AGENDA – Pink Noise (thegayagenda.bandcamp.com) We’ve heard it repeatedly from Christian Conservatives: “They’re trying to push the gay agenda into our lives!” But "they" don’t know what the real gay agenda is, and this San Diego queer hardcore band is here to give you a crash course. This is the band’s third release, and their second LP, after 2018’s self-titled double flexi-disc EP and 2020’s one-sided LP (it was on clear vinyl, with the B-side being a silk-screen of the band’s logo). Their short homocore blasts have typically been chaotic and noisy, like a lot of modern hardcore, but this new LP features more melody and better production quality, so you can really hear the songs. They’re still powerful and edgy, with speedy pounding songs, huge power chords, thumping bass lines, and angry vocals. You still best not try anything homophobic with them around, if you know what’s good for you. Because the gay agenda ain’t all about same sex love. For example, “Eye for an Eye” is about the new consequences for gay bashing. No, you won’t get away with it anymore, because it’s eye for an eye time, and they don’t intend to let you walk away. The gay agenda also includes encouraging people to be their authentic selves. “Sissy Boy,” which opens the LP, speaks to how queer boys have been told to act straight to be safe in the world, but how this causes conflict of self: “All the years spent hiding / I can no longer tell / Which face is truly my own / Or the lie I’ve used as a shield.” The music is angular and cuts like a knife, pounding unrelentingly. There’s a song about standing up for yourself (“Find Your Voice”), and a song about government silence during the AIDS crisis (“Vale of Tears”). There’s a refresher for young queers who weren’t alive before the Supreme Court struck down anti-sodomy laws or when states began legalizing same-sex marriage; “Hid the Truth” is about how in the post-World War II era of supposed growing freedom and prosperity for all Americans, gay people were still persecuted and prosecuted – it was illegal to be gay in many places. The title track is about the apolitical gays, who “want glitter with no political voice,” who just want to know “Who’s your favorite drag queen? What’s your drug of choice?” They reject militant political messages, because they’re no better than the Christian Nationalists in that they are only interested in associating with people like themselves, and they perpetrate the “straight-washing” of views that don’t match their own. Probably the most important song of the album is “Sigh of Relief.” It speaks to how all oppressed people need to stand together and fight for each other’s rights. Just because gay and lesbian people have earned some level of equal rights (for now) doesn’t mean sighing in relief and thinking the fight is over. You can’t say “It’s not my fight / When black lives killed by police.” You can’t say “It’s them not me / Don’t want to hear a speech / When Trans lives are killed in gay streets.” The song reminds us of the allies that fought for gay rights, and now we all need to work together to secure equal rights for everyone. Don’t say it’s not your fight because your skin is white or because you’re cis-gendered. And as the song that follows (“Architects”) says, we have to “Stop drawing lines in our community / Don’t argue with me about your selfish identity / Together we fight as a voice against impunity / Then why only Pride, do you claim our unity? / Disdainful of our sisters, we’re the architects of our own demise.” In other words, united we stand, divided we fall, as the old saying goes. With better sound quality, less chaos and more discernable melodic lines, and growled vocals in which you can actually hear the important words of the lyrics, Pink Noise is The Gay Agenda’s best release yet.![Image 14](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/surulin.jpg) ## SURALIN – Every Day Slices Me (itselevenrecords.bandcamp.com) After 17 years as a band and having released five LPs, Chemnitz, Germany-based Suralin are releasing their very first 7” EP! Chemnitz is located in the German state of Saxony, deep in the heart of the former German Democratic Republic (East Germany). It’s unlikely the members of the band have any memory of the period when their country was a Soviet satellite; they may well have not even been alive when Germany reunited in 1990. Their music, therefore, has none of the austerity one associates with Soviet era music. Indeed, there’s more resemblance to the Krautrock of the 1960s and 1970s with pounding minimalist rhythms. But they blend these rhythms with lush dreamy indie pop and create mesmerizing music. There’s an urgency to the four songs on the EP, which comes from that insistent rhythm. The guitars jangle vehemently, the bass thrumming away to the beat, but the vocals are smooth and beautiful. The A-side features two songs in this vein, “Driving Home” and the title track, and though the B-side songs are cohesive, they change things up somewhat. “The Sentiment’s a Lie” is a little slower and smoother, with a jazzy vibe. And “I Love a Boy” is harder and noisier, with a bigger, more open sound. This is a compelling EP that I highly recommend. * * * ![Image 15](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/antietam.jpg) ## ANTIETAM – The Counting Game (Dromedary Records, dromedaryrecords.bandcamp.com) Antietam is a storied name in the world of underground rock music. Founded more than four decades ago by guitarist/vocalist Tara Key and bassist Tim Harris, the band has evolved over time, through an early art punk and experimental spimd to raucous, punk-inspired indie. As with most of us, they’ve slowed things down over the years, and nowadays focus on ambient and folk-inspired tunes. And, to be very honest, I prefer their earlier music, because it was higher energy and had more vitality and adventure in it. _The Counting Game_, to my ears, is just too relaxed, feeling almost lackadaisical. The songs are smooth and flowy, but there’s not a lot of energy behind them. The textures are nice, with a dreamy post-punk sort of sound, but there’s also a lot of country twang, including banjo, and songs that drone repetitively. Even when they get grittier, like on “The Finest Line,” the pace drags, Tara Key shows she’s still a guitar master, and I do like some of the cool jazz tone of “Every Other Star,” but it just doesn’t feel like they’re excited to be playing these songs. Even on “Coco Bella,” which also uses jazz beats, trumpet, and piano, it just doesn’t have that verve I expected. This disappointed me. ![Image 16](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/Armsandarmor.jpg) ## ARMS & ARMOUR – The Hunted (Sweet Cheetah Records / Steadfast Records, steadfastrecords.com) Arms & Armour are the dystopian soundtrack of the modern world. The duo of Lauren Voss (vocals, guitar, and synths) and John Panza (drums, drum machine programming, guitar, and synths) play music that’s a mix of industrial, goth, doom, and icy cold post punk. Guitars are heavy and sludgy, the vocals melancholic, and the tempos are slow and deliberate. The result is the music that foretells of existential threat in a post-apocalyptic world. We hear the wind howling in the empty places, and echoes of the past that we all ignored that, had we listened, could have prevented the fate in which we find ourselves. Angular laments are juxtaposed against drum and bass beats, while guitar dissonance expresses how broken the world is. This is the slower drugged out vision that Future Sounds of London gave us on their _Dead Cities_ album. There’s something hypnotic and brooding in the music, something that gives succor in the bleakness of life. Hang in there. All is not lost. The album ends with a delicate sign of hope with “Ash’s Song.” Maybe this isn’t the end. Somber and reflective. ![Image 17](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/cuvabimo.jpg) ## CUVA BIMÖ – New Western Values (Sell the Heart Records, cuvabimo.bandcamp.com) They proudly call themselves a “post-whatever rock” band, and that is fairly apt for the Bay area quartet made up of Sebastian Moeller (guitar, vocals), Pete Vadelnieks (guitar, vocals), Jake Bilich (bass), and Ricky Cunliffe (drums). The band formed in response to a Craigslist ad, and considered calling themselves "Craigslist Hook Up,” but decide against it (for now). The band’s style is a mélange of post punk, indie, garage, noise rock, grunge, and art punk, exhibiting elements of all of these but falling solely into none of those camps. After the decidedly experimental instrumental, “4 A.M. Somewhere,” which opens the album, we get the quirky title track, which features grunge-filled guitars and bass, an angular melodic line, and eccentric vocal delivery. The track is chaotic and offbeat, with many unexpected twists and turns. It makes it my kind of track! And that’s the sort of thing we get throughout the ten tracks, gritty noisy instrumentals and vocals that are very much in the art punk vein. It’s like their genre is one of structured disorder. There’s chaos and mayhem, yet it’s controlled and managed to produce these songs. I like the powerful vocals and post punk melodic line of “Charm Offensive,” while “800 Meter Tears” mixes the art punk aesthetic with mathy goth guitars and funky bass. The minimalist melody of “Sound and Fury” is hypnotic, and the deep gravelly vocals are a stark contrast to the gliding instrumentals. Sounding very different, “Malagradecido” is sung in Spanish and has deep garage rock roots. And the closing track, “Too Much,” is not enough! It’s psych! It’s grunge! It’s art punk! It’s all of these and none of them! It’s the genius of CuVa Bimö! ![Image 18](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/wesleystace.jpg) ## WESLEY STACE – One Last Heist (Pravda Records, wesleystace.bandcamp.com) Previously recording under the name John Wesley Harding, Wesley Stace has reverted to his birth name more recently for his music. He’s also a well-known author of four novels, including the international best-seller _Misfortune_. He’s also recorded duets with Bruce Springsteen, Lou Reed, and Rosanne Cash, among others, and has created Cabinet of Wonders, a cabaret-style show that plays regularly in New York City and features a rotating cast of performers. He has taught at Princeton, Swarthmore, and Farleigh-Dickinson and writes for the Times Literary Supplement and the Wall Street Journal. It’s safe to say Stace is a modern day renaissance man. His UK origins (he was born in East Sussex) are on display in his music, which has a bit of 1980's Stiff Records vibe to it, and there’s also a little Billy Joel, a bit of Elvis Costello, and loads of old school jazzy pop music. A lot of the songs are quite clever or tell interesting stories, like the title track, which opens the album. The titular activity is what happens when a master thief is pulled in from retirement for one last job, and it immediately reminds me of the Stiff Records era, with a jazzier, smoother Ian Dury sound. It’s about taking that one last risk that, if it works out, will set you for your golden years, but if it doesn’t there could be dire consequences. Songs like “Penelope” are what give me the Elvis Costello impression, an ode to a woman with the same kind of lovely pop ballad, just a bit jazzed up. I enjoy the finger-snapping “Get It in Your Fingers,” a quietly hopping tune that features a circle of fifths chord progression at one point. “I Say Lots of Things” is a smooth song about a smooth talker who lies easily and takes advantage of the good nature of others. And “Thoughts and Prayers” is simply a wonderful piano ballad, about how people put blinders on and don’t care to do anything about the misfortunes of others until it happens to them. It’s about how politicians do nothing but offer “thoughts and prayers,” leaving people to continue suffering. A lovely album. ![Image 19](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/STETSONHEATSEEKER.jpg) ## STETSON HEAT SEEKER – This Is No Place for Cowards (stetsonheatseeker.bandcamp.com) Stetson Heat Seeker is a newer band, formed in 2023 in Seattle, Washington. They quickly released a mini-LP and began playing shows around town, and then went though a series of personnel changes leading us to the current lineup of Ian Read (lead vocals, guitar), Megan Slavich (bass, backing vocals), Joshua Ihler (drums, percussion, backing vocals), Katie Cassidy (tenor sax, lead and backing vocals), and Madison Moilanen (guitar, tambourine, backing vocals). Given the band name and the sound, you might be forgiven for thinking they’re from Texas, because they’ve got a distinctly cow-punk vibe, but it’s heavy frenetic stuff, mixing in a bit of surf punk, and the tenor sax gives the songs are powerfully gritty and soulful sound. The lead vocals are manic and strong, and the overall sound reminds me of China’s Round Eye, but maybe with a funkier edge. The overall tone is sharp and biting, with loads of fuzz in the bass, and the energy level is off the charts. Heat seeking indeed! These cowboys are the kind that’ll come home covered in dust and dirt and aren’t afraid to mix it up and get into some trouble. “Cultbreaker” is a perfect opener, strong and dark controlled chaos. There’s a great loping ode to working hard while remaining in poverty with “Minimum Wage.” There’s more not-giving-a-fuck than anger, and plenty of sarcasm. I really like the surfy garage punk vibes of “Sharpshooter,” a song about the stupid risks people take, often in pursuit of sex or love, using a sharpshooter show as a metaphor. The pursuit of feeling good (if you know what I mean) is the topic of the super sleazy “Oh Sweet Pain,” with a repeating riff and lyrics that’ll have you jonesing for what it is you want. And “Trouble Finds You,” the penultimate track, is a solid standout, with a dark, evil, twisted circus sound. If you get cold, don’t worry about seeking heat, seek this record instead. ![Image 20](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/stillinsane.jpg) ## STILL INSANE – When Friendship Is Not Enough (Thousand Islands Records, thousandislandsrecords.ca) This record is a perfect example of why putting one of the best tracks first is so important. When I first started listening to the first track, “Intro,” and even the title track that follows, my reaction was that this band sounds like that local hardcore band from the outer edges of the metro area that’s populated by older dudes who never outgrew the 1980's. You know the ones, the guys who still wear mohawks in their 50's and 60's and who only listen to early 80's hardcore on repeat. They’re awful, but they open for every touring hardcore band that comes through town. We all have ‘em. I almost gave up on the record, but that’s not me, I give everything a fair chance. Good thing I did, because the quality improved dramatically. That intro made me think this was going to be some metallic prog-rock band, while the title track is generic thrashy speed-core with out-of-tune gang vocals singing the chorus, which consists of just the name of the song. The lead vocals are spoken-shouted in a fairly generic “hardcore” way. It’s honestly a mess. As the album progresses, though, the songs improve. There’s loping poppy crunchy punk rock in “Do What You Want” and “Missed It Again,” which are couple of the best tracks of the album, but most of it features dark, speedy, 90's skate-punk. The instrumentals are well done, but the one thing that bothered me is that the vocals are a little problematic, with some pitch issues. ![Image 21](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/strangebirds.jpg) ## STRANGE BIRDS – Little Victories (Sweet Cheetah Records, strangebirdssongs.bandcamp.com) Back in the 90's, I remember Louisville as having some good bands that featured an emo or post hardcore sound. Bands like Metroschifter, Shipping News, Sunspring, Slint, and more were putting out great records. Strange Birds adds to this legacy, though featuring a transplant from Kansas City, Missouri. Brandon Butler, the guitarist and vocalist, is better known from his time in Boys Life, while drummer Ella Jean Jumpkins and bassist Brian Meurer are homegrown talents, having grown up playing in bands in the local Louisville scene (note, this recording features Matt Olsen on bass). The songs on this LP have a subdued, pensive quality, as one might expect given their homebase and pedigree. But even within this they’ve got a wide range of sounds going on. The album opens with jangly indie pop in the title track, and immediately after we get the understated indie blended with a bit of Americana of “BMX Summer” and “Take You Anywhere.” “The Old House” starts out with a striding indie sound, but as the song evolves, the guitar takes on a bit of 80s goth tone for a time. I really like “Darker Still,” which is one of the more wistful songs, starting tentatively, but getting thicker and more emphatic as the song grows. The use of a guitar wailing in the background is very effective at setting a tone, as are the whispery vocals. As the song fades out, there are ghostly whispers and ambient sounds, providing an air of mystery. “Roll with the Punches” feels out of place after that. It’s another pleasant slow head-bobber that mixes hazy indie with an Americana twang that fits in better with the earlier part of the album. But it’s with the penultimate track, “Blood Currents,” that the album hits its heights, in my opinion. It’s the most experimental track of the album, featuring a meandering melody and a spoken word track buried in the mix that consists of deep buzzing bass, softly tentative drums, and lush guitars. It’s a gorgeous sonic piece of art. The album closes with “Deleted Scenes,” which brings in a noisy indie sound and a song about the dismantling of the “American Dream,” and how it’s become nothing but a series of “deleted scenes,” everything good about life being cut away from us. I miss listening to the music coming out of Louisville. But now we have Strange Birds, and they’re a worthy heir to the mantle.![Image 22](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/thermals2.jpg) ## THE THERMALS – Under Crushing Rain (Static Catsup Aspic, thethermals.bandcamp.com) OMG, they’re back! The Portland band that was formed way back in 2002, survived multiple lineup changes and formally disbanded in 2018 has returned, now as a solo project of founder Hutch Harris. The band was much beloved in their heyday, releasing seven studio LPs and a bunch of EPs and singles. They played a mix of pop punk-influenced indie rock and indie pop. I remember seeing them play live on multiple occasions, and thinking they were a pleasant enough band, but too many of their songs sounded alike to my ears to be a real stand-out band. Now, ten years after the release of their last album, _We Disappear_, and after the December 2025 announcement of Harris’ return as The Thermals, a new album, _Under the Crushing Rain,_ brings the return of The Thermals. And while the music is not quite as lo-fi as the band was known for, the poppy punk-informed indie rock is still there. Harris’ unique vocal stylings are still there. But what’s great about this album is that, even though the sound is still distinctly The Thermals, there’s more variety in the ten songs offered here than I ever remember hearing when they were a touring band. The music still features emphatic rhythms, but the tone varies from the darkness of “Good Morning Fellow Scavengers” to the incongruently bright “Dark, Dark Place,” the latter being a bouncy song about wanting to both eschew the past, but not to erase it, to sit with it, experience it, but not get stuck in it. There are songs that, while slower, have a stronger bounce and a soulful feel, like “Spirit Collectors,” and there are songs that are breezy folky pop, like “In the Flow.” I love the clean guitar tone on this one, especially in the short guitar solo, and Harris’ vocals give it a nerd-pop vibe that’s appealing. There’s 50’s early rock and roll thing going on with “I Will Be Delivered,” and the title track that closes the LP is an impossibly happy sounding song with very dark lyrics. The variety, the arrangements that feature strong keyboards, and the solid songwriting mean that not only are The Thermals back, it means Harris has released the best Thermals album yet. Now he needs to recruit some people to take this show on the road! ![Image 23](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/firesalecorpsplit.jpg) ## FIRE SALE / THE CORPS – Split Decision split EP (Negative Progression Records, www.negativeprogressionrecords.com) Two bands, two sides, two songs each are what we get on this new split EP featuring Fire Sale and The Corps. Fire Sale features seasoned veterans from familiar bands: Pedro Aida from Ann Beretta, ShotClock, and The Iron Roses takes up vocal duties; Chris Swinney of The Ataris, Brazil, and Underminded is the lead guitarist; Matt Riddle (Face to Face, No Use for a Name, Pulley) is the bassist; Brad Edwards (Weaver Street) plays rhythm guitar; and Matt Morris (Darlington, Down By Law) is on drums. Their tracks sound just like you might imagine coming from a supergroup lineup like this: powerful, melodic, and crunchy. Their first track, “Kill the Noise,” is a dark loping track that speaks about mental health, while the politically charged “Dies Irae” is a little poppier, a little faster, and more frantic, in a Descendents sort of vein. Flipping the record over reveals two tracks from Vancouver’s The Corps. They may be lesser known, but they’ve been around for over a decade, and they offer up a couple of speedy skate-punk tracks in a 90's vein. The music is fast and crisp, yet always melodic. Their first song, “Imposter Syndrome,” is an ode to something we all feel from time to time, some more than others. In the case of The Corps, it’s about sharing the stage with their musical heroes (they’ve toured with Ignite and Strung Out, for example) and feeling unworthy. The second track is a little smoother and introspective, and arguably better. “Another World” is one of the band’s comic-book inspired songs (apparently many of their songs are inspired by comics, particularly the DC Universe). Solid split. * * * ![Image 24](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/ballyhoo.jpg) ## BALLYHOO! – Bad Summer (Right Coast Records, www.rightcoastrecords.com) Maryland band Ballyhoo! have been making music for the past three decades. They’ve been described as a “reggae rock” band, but this album is almost entirely slick 1990s/2000s pop punk in the vein of stalwarts of the era like Blink 182 or Sum 41. Which makes sense when you note that this new album was produced by John Feldmann, who’s produced Blink, as well as Good Charlotte, Panic! At the Disco, Avril Lavigne, and Goldfinger (his own band). It’s the slick generic pop punk sound that filled the airwaves in the 90s and early 2000s, and, as such, does nothing for me. And I guess there’s some mild reggae-pop on the record, but it’s super watered down and whitewashed. “Cali Girl” and “Long Weekend” fall into this category, but it’s about the only music even close to reggae on the album. “Happy” features a couple of alto saxophone solos that makes the song sound like something from the SNL band. And “I Guess I’ll Go Fuck Myself” is really unfortunate song that wishes harm on others, with lyrics that include “I still wish you would die.” I guess it’s about people who troll on the internet, and cause emotional distress to others, but still… If you’re a Blink fan, you may like this record, but I’m not a fan. ![Image 25](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/generacion.jpg) ## GENERACIÓN SUICIDA – Hombre Nuevo (Vitriol Records, www.vitriolrecords.com) Generación Suicida, hailing from Los Angeles, presents a dark, dusty lonely sort of post punk vision. The band shows their garage punk roots on some songs, with some rapid downstroke strumming, but most of the songs have a slower, more introspective feel, filled with atmosphere. The songs are all sung in Spanish, so it’s hard to for me to know what they’re singing about. But most of the songs sure are morose. Some, though, have a more urgent feel, like “Desilucion,” sung with gritty vocals to give it an edge. The title translates to “Disillusion” or “Disappointment,” so take your cue from that as to what the song is about. It’s not a happy thing. “Oscuridad” is one of those garage punk tunes, with a livelier feel and a quicker pace. But the gorgeous reverb-laden guitar gives it that mournful sound, appropriate for a song whose title means “Darkness.” “Golpe Al Barrio” (Blow to the Neighborhood), too, has a bit more bounce to it, but it also has a menacing tone. Things are not looking up in the barrio, that’s for sure. One of my favorite songs of the album is “Tres.” It’s a simple enough song, but there’s some cool tension effects from the guitars inserted into the music, and a dark surf punk melodic line. And that surf guitar sound returns on “A Los ue Deje Atras” (To Those I Left Behind), which closes the album. The ten songs fully convey a sense of despair – it’s not necessary to understand Spanish to get the emotional content of these songs. Generación Suicida paint a bleak picture of the present, and offer little hope for the future. Recommended. ![Image 26](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/hovland.jpg) ## HOLSMAN – Sally (theholsman.bandcamp.com) Holsman is the eponymous Chicago band led by Ryan Holsman and Dan Tinkler. _Sally_ is a concept album that explores the pair’s experiences as victims of child abuse and how that impacts their abilities to form relationships in adulthood. For example, the lead single, “I’ll Be a Dog in My Next Life” speaks to how even coming back as a dog is no guarantee of a happy life. We all think of pets as receiving unconditional love, but shitty people are always shitty, even kicking their dog, as described in the song. Even the promise that “I’ll be a good boy” is no guarantee of decent treatment, as the song recounts being left alone for hours and feeling that everything bad that happens is your own fault. The band plays a brand of punk-inspired indie rock, with full-on melodies and lush arrangements, vocals packing an emotional wallop. Think Against Me! or a more engaging version of Menzingers. There’s a rawness to the music, a sharp edge to the songs, and they cut deep. You can sense the explosive temper in “Tantrum,” vocals and music going from calm to intense shouting and violence and back again, while always remaining fully tuneful. I really like the opening track, “God’s Drunkest Driver,” which tells a story about Sally, giving the album its title. It uses a '60's pop rock melody and contrasts it with a gruff grunge arrangement. And “Silent Protagonist” alternates between powerful grunge and smoother indie rock. An outlier, sounding very different from the other tracks, is “Perfect! Thank You!” It’s a smoother breezier sound, with lyrics about how, in our adult lives, we do all sorts of things to put on a façade, a false image to the rest of the world, hiding our pains and anxieties from others, using chemicals to maintain the ruse. Listening to these songs makes me want to give Holsman a hug and tell him everything will be OK. This is a solidly good debut LP. ![Image 27](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/jayhawks.jpg) ## THE JAYHAWKS – Sanctuary Park (jayhawksofficial.com) The Jayhawks are a long-standing (on-again, off-again) band that formed over four decades ago in Minneapolis. They’ve had a couple of hiatuses in the intervening years, but here they are, back with another release to add to their massive catalog. They’ve been labeled an “alternative country rock” band in the past, and sure, about half of the songs on _Sanctuary Park_ have a twang, but I hear a lot of influence from power-pop and even indie-rock in this album, showing how they remain a vital and evolving band even after all this time. The arrangements are lush, with multi-part vocal harmonies, acoustic and electric guitars, and keyboards. Country rock songs include “Mr. Lincoln,” which has a Beatles meets honky-tonk vibe, and “Hands Upon the Wheel,” which includes some subtle steel pedal guitar and a dark storytelling sound. “Leap of Faith” is straight-up honky-tonk, with piano, mandolin, and accordion, sounding like something that we might have heard on the old Prairie Home Companion radio show. But other songs are much more power-pop and indie, and more to my tastes. “Keeping Our Heads Above Water” and “Kingston Girl,” the opening pair of tracks on the LP, have a great '80's alternative rock sound, nice and smooth. “American Midnight” is a favorite, for its breezy sound that straddles between alt-country and indie. Then there’s the title track, with a completely different sound than anything else on the album, with a mix of Pink Floyd smooth psych and folk rock storytelling. The Jayhawks are that rare band from way back when that aren’t content to rest on their laurels and just play the old “hits,” and who want to keep making new music. And I’m here for that. ![Image 28](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/startercar.jpg) ## STARTER CAR – Afterlight (startercar.bandcamp.com) Here’s an album from another band that’s been called “country-influenced,” but I don’t see it at all here. What I hear is gorgeously understated indie with hints of folk influence. The pretty arrangements belie the dark subject matter, such as on the opening track, “Throwing Down,” which is about how one might spiral out of control when finding one’s self alone for the weekend. “I’m in trouble when I’m not around you / I drink doubles when I’m not around you,” the song opens. The easy relaxed lope of the song is at odds with the tailspin of bad choices. The songs feature a lovely blend of acoustic and electric instruments, giving the songs a contemplative sound, something appropriate for the self-examination of the songs. I love how “Avert” starts out so quietly, with throbbing guitar lines, and how it grows to a huge emotional swell by the end of the track. I adore the breezy “Wisecrack,” with guitar and violin intertwining and echoing the melody. And right after is the jaunty waltz time “More Me.” This pair of tracks are probably my favorites of the album, and placing them together is brilliant tracking. Overall, I really like the relaxed yet introspective vibe of these songs. Nicely done. ![Image 29](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/johnvanderslice.jpg) ## JOHN VANDERSLICE – Focus (johnvanderslice.bandcamp.com) John Vanderslice has declared he was done writing song lyrics. “I have nothing more to say,” he announced. Recently having relocated from Los Angeles to The Netherlands, his wife Maria convinced him that he should continue singing and writing music, and she would write the lyrics. So the pair teamed up with producer James Riotto and set up about making this album filled with a compelling mix of electric and acoustic, with synths, saxophone, and guitar.
