Experimental and traditional songcraft collide and meld together. Vanderslice had spent time experimenting with electronic music, and though it’s nice to have his voice back, it was time well-spent. The synths give a nice texture to the songs, from an avant garde edge to lush arrangements. It gives the songs a unique twist and that bit of “extra.” I love the opening track, “From the Life of Marionettes,” which blends acoustic guitars with lush flutes and saxophones and off-kilter electronic interjections. There a cool bossa nova undercurrent to the track, too, particularly in the rhythm and percussion. It’s a wonderful reintroduction, and a gorgeous new sound. The song was inspired by an Ingmar Bergman film John and Maria watched, and warns the listener of the untrustworthiness of the narrator/singer. There are lines that seem both meaningless and profound at the same time, like “I speak in words and colors I cannot see.” There’s a dark dusty vibe in “Steep Land Surveyor,” Vanderslice’s voice sometimes cracking with emotion, the upright bass giving the song a wonderful warmth, adding a hint of jazziness to the arrangement. There are some wonderful instrumentals here, too, including the tentative sounds of “Chopped Piano,” featuring cut up and reassembled bits of piano, synth, and melodic vocalizations. There’s a confessional quality to “Chasing My Blues,” with a melancholy ballad quality and lyrics like “I’ve done drugs my whole life /As much or as little as I like / But this might be the end of the line.” The song seems to be about trying to be better, with the refrain, “Chasing my blues away.” The closing track, “Hold My Head,” is jaw-dropping, with the sound of a post-apocalyptic science-fiction soundtrack. And “jaw-dropping” is a good descriptor for the whole album. It’s that good. ![Image 30](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/vista%20blue%20champtions.jpg) ## VISTA BLUE – Championship of Love (wearevistablue.bandcamp.com) Vista Blue are back, stronger than ever, putting out new songs with furious frequency! And we’re all the better for that. And because Vista Blue’s Mike Patton loves topical tunes, this time out the opening of college football season is the inspiration for songs that use football as a metaphor for relationships. The signature Vista Blue buzzy guitars, keyboards, and Ramones-core vibe are on full display in the pair of tracks that feature a mid-tempo pace and Patton’s casual yet sincere vocals. The “A” side title track is about relationships as competition and trying to figure out a winning strategy, while the “B” side, “She’s My Taysom Hill,” likens romantic love to sports idol worship (Taysom Hill is an NFL player with the New Orleans Saints, and previously played for the Green Bay Packers and the BYU Cougars in college). New Vista Blue songs are always welcome, even when they come fast and furious! ![Image 31](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/winelips.jpg) ## WINE LIPS – TV Dinner (Stomp Records, stomprecords.com) What happens when you mix garage rock, psych, and punk rock? You get Wine Lips, of course! You get 13 hard-driving tracks of manic music, with a frenetic pace and explosive energy. Lo-fi recording and snotty attitude are the order of the day, and the band is like a mainlined injection of adrenaline to remind you that you’re still alive. This is the music your mother warned you about, it’s the seedy club down the alley that smells of urine and weed. It’s all the good times you’ve ever thought about but can’t remember, because of course you can’t remember that night. Though most of the songs are speedy, crunchy, and sassy, “Trip to the Doctor” slows things down; it’s the morning after hangover, until you use the meds the “doctor” gives you to wake you back up, and it starts speeding with more power and energy. One of the most psychedelic tracks of the album is “Leech.” Though it’s still down and dirty garage grit, there’s a definite '60's psych vibe injected into the veins of this beast, and it’s like a warm wave washing over a frozen shoreline. And “Giant Man Baby,” too, is loaded with psych characteristics and gives the impression the we’re listening to the music in the static between two radio stations as we explore the universe by looking through both ends of a telescope at the same time. “Thirst Trap” snaps you back to reality, but you suddenly realize that something’s gone horribly wrong in your absence of mind, and you need to catch up fast! But you’re falling further and further behind, even as you keep running faster and faster. The high cost of living is decried in “Semi Detached Furnished Home,” with complaints about not being able to afford, rent, groceries, or gas. I love the frigid shimmer that yields to the hard rocking nature of “Fried V,” and we’re brought back to that seedy urine and weed soaked alley with “Strip Club DJ,” with its cheesy sleezy glamour: “Twenty bucks is all it takes / It won’t last long but it sure feels great! / If you do it right you can get on stage / Someone check his balls, is he doing OK?” After listening to this record, my balls are more than OK. Highly recommended! * * * ![Image 32](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/deadsealords.jpg) ## DEAD SEA LORDS – "God Can’t Count" EP (Belladonna Records, belladonna-records.com) Noisy and chaotic, yet eminently emotional and powerful, would be one way to describe Gainesville’s Dead Sea Lords. This six-song EP follows their 2024 self-titled debut LP, pretty much picking up where they left off. The music drives hard, but it also throbs hypnotically. I hear elements of early Midwest emo and late period hardcore, giving the songs a definite mid-to-late 80s vibe. But the distortion and anarchic tumult give the songs a vital modern edge. The performances are so raw and energetic, the record sounds more like a live show than a studio recording. ![Image 33](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/getarounds.jpg) ## THE GET AROUNDS – Going Out Tonight (thegetaroundsarenumber1. bandcamp.com) The Get Arounds are one of many bands formed during the COVID pandemic. They began with songwriter and guitarist Carman Lethbridge and drummer Lana Ryma starting to write together, and with Ryma deciding to come out from behind the drumkit and become the lead vocalist. Jay Solyom was recruited to take the drumming spot, with Lethbridge multitasking on guitar, bass, keyboards and backing vocals (the live lineup also features Sean Stubbs, Lisa Lloyd, and Kimi Mah)._Going Out Tonight_ is the band’s sophomore LP, following 2023’s _I Wanna Live_. It features a baker’s dozen tracks that range widely, from hard rock to power pop, glam rock, and even into indie rock territory. The huge variety makes the album feel a little disjointed, with some really solid songs and some that fall miserably flat. One rule I learned a long time ago about tracking albums is always put one of your best songs first. It’s the way you can capture a listener’s attention and the way to get music critics to keep listening. The Get Arounds have not heeded this advice, because “Fuck Around” is a hard rock mess with vocal tuning problems. Nevertheless, I kept listening. The first half of the album is nothing to write home about, sounding more like a high school rock and roll band than a group of professional musicians. Tempos are lazy, and the music feels like stale leftovers from the 70s. “Waiting for the Stars” is no better that the first track. And “Kill or Be Killed” is super cheesy. The arrangements in most of the first half of the album are too thin and there’s just not much energy in the songs. The title track may be the worst offender of the album in this respect. One exception is “Bones,” which is more of an 80s pop rock ballad. It sounds very different from the other tracks in this part of the record, and the vocals are more tuneful, so it’s more successful. But once we get to the second half of the album, things begin to improve. The songs drop the hard rock pretense and focus on more of an indie rock sound, with better sounding vocals and smoother arrangements. “Black Corvette” takes things up a notch from the preceding tracks, and “Hideaway” is a real standout with a poppy punky indie rock vibe and just a bit of 80s influence. “Do Or Die” mixes dark power pop with indie rock, and is another pleaser. Unfortunately, the last few tracks of the album return to more of the cheesy hard rock sound. I just couldn’t get into this. ![Image 34](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/mental%20gymnast.jpg) ## MENTAL GYMNAST – "EP2" (Say-10 Records, www.say-10.com) Mental Gymnast is really hitting the ground running. After releasing their debut EP this past winter, they’re back with five more songs of crunchy old-school hardcore meets synth-punk. Dark melodies, angry vocals, and big gang vocals mix with manic synths to create something that reminds me of Artless, the 80s hardcore band fronted by Maximum Rock’n’Roll’s Mykel Board. And once again they pack a lot into a short amount of time; the five songs occupy a mere six and a half minutes. We get the obsessive “Romance Novels,” with the verses narrated like a twisted story and the chorus gang shouted, the synths swirling around madly and the guitars, bass, and drums providing a solid crunch. I like the hollow sound of “I Want to Believe,” and the crazed speed and screaming of “The Lowest Bar.” Mental Gymnast hasn’t played much in the way of shows yet, but here’s hoping they start touring, because this is much better than a lot of modern hardcore that’s just noise and incoherent screaming. ![Image 35](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/newagehealers-blowingsmoke.jpg) ## NEW AGE HEALERS – Blowing Smoke Through the Choir (newagehealers.bandcamp.com) New Age Healers is a Seattle band that defies the norm for the Pacific Northwest. Where most bands from that region tend toward heavy, gritty grunge and similar subgenres, New Age Healers dabble in a variety of other sounds, but focus on variations on shoegaze. In the past they’ve blended heavy sounds and psychedelia; on this LP, I hear a mix of shoegaze and indie pop. It’s lighter than past records, for the most part, and supremely pleasant. I love the opening track, “The Fastest Slow,” for that very reason. That’s not to say the band has completely given up psych or heavier sounds; those are here, too, but in smaller, more palatable doses. “Falling Apart” has some of both, to a degree. And “Ultra” really brings harder edgier sounds, but mixing in spacey vocoder style vocal treatments and guitar tone. The whole track has a hypnotic sort of style. “You’re the Sun” has some heaviness, too, with a hard driving low end and deliberate rhythm, and the song has a great melodic bounce, too. And “Devotion” blows the whole thing out of the water, eschewing the shoe-gaze aesthetic for a raucous post punk tune that’ll really get you jumping around. I really like the ethereal folk-pop sounds that are mixed into “Sunday Bed,” a song featuring guest vocals from Valerie Green. I am enjoying the evolution that band has displayed; the textures of these new songs are gorgeous and they’re varied enough to provide sonic stimulation and hold interest. That’s one thing that’s really tough to do with shoegaze, because sometimes the songs tend to all sound alike. Not so with _Blowing Smoke Through the Choir_, which I think is New Age Healers’ best album yet. ![Image 36](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/reserver.jpg) ## RESERVER – Reserver (Funambulist Recording Company) I’ve listened to this album about a dozen times over the course of a weekend and it’s left me dumbfounded. It’s the rare album that gets better and better on each subsequent listen, and this is one. It’s hard to describe the music, because there’s so much going on and yet it’s also so simple.Imagine combining the thick guitar noise of Jesus and Mary Chain with the melancholy of Joy Division, complete with baritone lead vocals. And the melancholy is real. Frontman Chad Preston stepped away from his previous band, The Laureates, when his wife Kerri was diagnosed with cancer. She sadly succumbed to her illness, but Preston got through those difficult years by writing songs, and with former Laureates bandmates Adam Penly and Crawfie Ward (guitar and bass, respectively) and drummer Dan Wendt, there was a drive to record those songs. As they say, they are a testament to the healing power of music. Right from the start, we’re in the thick of things. “Heart Is a Bomb” speaks to the inevitability of the loss of a loved one and the devastating impact that can have. I love the frantic guitar riffs and the somber bass lines, and the fatalism of the lyrics wrecked me (“Yesterday’s Papers uncovered the plot / Conclusion is coming, ready or not / The gods didn’t download your prayers or your thoughts / Sooner or later you’re here then you’re not.”) Another favorite is “Parallax,” a song that melds the sound of Joy Division with Mission of Burma’s style of song structure. Really, every one of the songs on this debut is a favorite, because they’re all so good. But it’s the mix of darkness and brightness of “Pyramids” that I think is the real stand-out. “I once said I wanna miss you / You know I do, you know I do / Someday I want to remember / You know I do / You know I do / I built this tomb to conceal you / It’s all for you, it’s all for you / You once said I won’t deceive you / I know you do, I know you do / But now you’re the sunshine.” The verses are the sad memories, but that one line chorus, “But now you’re the sunshine,” leaves me choked up. Music really does have healing properties. ![Image 37](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/ruckus.jpg) ## RUCKUS (Drunken Sailor Records, www.drunkensailorrecords.co.uk) When punk rock first emerged in the late 70's, it wasn’t fast and loud already. It began as a raw, simpler version of rock 'n' roll. And Boston’s Ruckus perfectly capture that loose feel, with power pop and good time rock and roll influences abounding. There’s a garage rock undercurrent, which fits perfectly with that early punk vibe, and you can just feel how much fun these guys are having playing the songs. Listening to the raucous music and the gritty throaty vocals on “Talk Ain’t Cheap Enuff,” you might forgive yourself for thinking you’ve falling through a time warp into a pub in 1978 London. Or listening to “Hot in the City,” you can feel the mix of influences of bands like The Jam and Ziggy Stardust era David Bowie. With Ruckus’ debut EP, they’ve recaptured the fun of rock and roll. * * * ![Image 38](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/gale%20forces.jpg) ## GALE FORCES – “Diviner” single (galeforces.bandcamp.com) A new standalone single from LA’s Gale Forces features heavy sounds with a Seattle influence, though the song also has the sound of 90's and 2000's alternative rock. There’s an emotional vibe to the song, which frontman Jade Devitt says was inspired by his partner challenging him to become more open and vulnerable in their relationship. He describes the experience as “frightening, but ultimately liberating.” The arrangement is already thick and lush, but I could imagine this being even better with strings and a less sludgy guitar tone. There’s a deliberate, slow pace to the song, pleading vocals, and an ending that’s unresolved. It’s an interesting listen. ![Image 39](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/kyeal.jpg) ## KYE ALFRED HILLIG – Widowmaker Express (kyealfredhillig.bandcamp.com) Imagine mixing Americana, folk, and moody indie-rock. The music is melancholy, with spare arrangements featuring guitars (acoustic and electric,) piano, drums, strings, and ethereal synths. This is the tenth LP from the Tacoma, Washington singer-songwriter Kye Alfred Hillig, and he says it was written in the wake of a health scare. He describes the album as a “breakup letter to the universe.” It’s an album, he says, that “wrestles with grief, faith, and the difficult work of carrying on.” The album is quite somber, with the hollow sound of reverb, Hillig’s vocals filled with uneasiness and anxiety. From the start, on “Oh Magic,” there’s a sense of loneliness and even despair. It starts with the gentle strumming of an acoustic guitar and Hillig’s singing, but some angelic backing vocals and piano join in subtly and delicately. And songs like “Coyote Skins” and “Fates Been Calling Through the Noise” feature otherworldly ambience set against soulful folk. There’s a bit of twang in some songs, courtesy of the lap steel guitar contributions of Graig Markel. And the strings on “The Ghost Will Turn Around” lend an almost spiritual quality to the song. But it might be “Indryd James” that steals the show here. The arrangement is incredibly delicate and understated, and the vocals convey a profound sense of loss. ![Image 40](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/iron%20filings.jpg) ## IRON LININGS – Urban Abyss (The Ghost Is Clear Records, theghostisclearrecords.com) Missouri’s Iron Linings formed in 2020, amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, and quickly recorded and released a debut EP to introduce themselves to the world. Following this was a split LP with Seaxes in 2022, and now comes their debut full-length. The band channels 90's post-hardcore noise blended with hard-hitting metal. The songs are frantic, filled with dissonance and unrelenting power. Rhythms constantly shift, vocals are shouted with intense ire, and unresolved tension fills every available moment of every song. As a result, each track, taken on its own, delivers an incendiary message, intended to spur movement and action. We get a mix of emo-core melodic lines, metallic riffs, and severely angular guitar jabs. The melodic friction generates fierce heat and catharsis. Taken together, the 12 tracks and more than 40 minutes of non-stop rage is overwhelming. Maybe too much. But I do like the riffs and interplay of the guitars and bass on “Red Mercury,” which has some moments that remind me of Circus Lupus. If you enjoy this sort of heavy hard-hitting metallic post-hardcore style, you’ll enjoy Iron Linings. ![Image 41](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/prisoner.jpg) ## PRISONER - Prisoner (Wicked Cool Records, www.wickedcoolrecords.com) What a ridiculously fun album! With 17 tracks and nearly an hour of music, you would think a couple of things: first, that the album is bloated and gets boring, and second, that this is a seasoned band that’s been around for a long time. You would be wrong on both counts. This is Prisoner’s debut LP, and it’s the furthest thing from boring you can get. They play an awesome mix of garage, synth pop, surf, and Stereolab-style psyche-pop, very atmospheric and very cinematic in style. Many of the songs remind me of 60's TV or movie soundtracks, especially those that had a Mod edge to them. And it’s either ironic or purposeful that the band’s name is “Prisoner,” because some of the music reminds me of the soundtrack to the short-lived but influential Patrick McGoohan TV show, _The Prisoner_. The album starts out with the high energy “La femme qui s’e´tait faite toute seule,” mixing retro psyche and garage, with instrumental music mixed with wild vocals in both French and English. It really sets a great tone for the album. I adore the breezy “Je ne retiendrai que toi,” with spoken vocals, muted trumpet, and a mysterious sound. “Borne pour obe´ir” is out of this world, with intense heavenly soprano operatic vocals and a cool Stereolab vibe, and “Il nous faudrait une bonne guerre” has a similar sound, though much more somber and melancholy. Some tracks are primarily instrumentals, some not. Many feature those intense operatic vocals. Many have horns, like “L’enfant qui est en moi parle,” which features trombone, and also synths tuned to sound like a harpsichord. It has a very dark mysterious sound, like the soundtrack to a 60s spy movie, but also has some great raucous garage rock moments. “Le paradis perdu,” or “Paradise Lost” is one of those instrumentals with operatic vocals, and the title is perfect because you can hear the loveliness of the paradise, but you can also hear the sadness and longing in the music. “Le village olympique” has a great psych-garage vitality about it, and the guitar tone and the trombone remind me again of “The Prisoner” TV show. Honestly, I can’t think of another band making music quite like this, and it’s just so much fun! They’re from France, and I sure hope they plan a US tour and come to San Diego, because I’ll buy a ticket to that! ![Image 42](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/rufio.jpg) ## RUFIO – From the Outside (Double Helix Records, doublehelixrecords.com) In the wake of major labels signing bands like Blink 182 and Sum 41 (which were, themselves, reactions to Green Day’s success), pop punk bands were in demand in the early 2000's. Enter Rufio, formed in 2000 in Southern California and named after the leader of the Lost Boys in the film _Hook_. Rufio were signed to Nitro Records in 2003, and released a couple of well-regarded albums. The mid-2000's brought tumultuous times for the band, with the departure of two members and their ultimate breakup. The following years saw sporadic reunion attempts, a “final farewell” show in 2007, and more shows in 2008 and 2009. Another new album followed in 2010, with plans for a world tour. And then the band called it quits yet again. One more reunion happened in 2015, and then… silence. But now, in 2026, the band decided to reissue an early hit, “Dipshit,” from their debut LP. And then they also announced brand new music, in the form of this five-song EP. And if you’re a fan of the sort of complex melodic pop punk of the 2000's, with simple poppy melodies and technical guitar work, you’ll love this EP. There’s skate-punk worthy speed on the title track and on “The Worst,” with intricate metallic riffs and super sweet pop melodies that would be right at home in a big arena. Other songs, like “Maps” or “Last Goodbye,” feature less speed and more slick production. They all feature those sugary strains. I have a lot of friends who will go wild for this. It’s a little too slick and commercial sounding for my tastes, though. ![Image 43](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/sleights-allover.jpg) ## THE SLEIGHTS – Don’t Worry It Will All Be Over Soon (Rad Girlfriend Records, www.radgirlfriendrecords.com) Colorado Springs’ The Sleights are turning into quite a prolific band! Since last year’s spring release of their previous LP, _This One’s Gonna Hurt_, they released the "Atari" EP last fall and a split with Land of Wolves just a few months ago. But I am not going to complain when the output is this good. And they really seem to be finding their groove with _Don’t Worry It Will All_ Be Over Soon. The music has a great aggressive edge that’s tempered by great melodies. It’s hard to call them pop-punk, because they’ve got such a hard-driving sound, but the melodic content is undeniable, too. It’s just that they’re perfectly balanced. The opening track, “LSD,” has a powerful hard rocking sound, and lyrics that may be less about a bad acid trip and more about ignoring the advice of friends. Feelings of loneliness and inadequacy are explored in the loping “After All,” and the end of a relationship is mourned in the grand and lovely “Wasted Time,” which I think may be my favorite song of the album. It has a sadness to it, and the ending is so beautiful, with a short high-pitched guitar solo. And though the topic of “The Void” may be a tough one to think about - our own demise - the music is bouncy and fun. The shortest and funniest track is “BODAP,” which stands for “Brian Ostrow drives a Prius.” It’s an 11 second hardcore blast that tells us what kind of car Brian Ostrow drives. As the album evolves it just keeps getting better, with “Alone” and “Empty Head,” which appear near the end of the record being a couple more favorites. The former is one of the punchier songs with a more aggressive edge, and the latter sounds like it could have come from a Chicago band, with its burly guitar sound. Though most of the songs are personal in nature, there’s politics here, too. This is a punk album, after all. “Drowning” is powerful and explosive, with angry gritty vocals singing about how both “the left” and “the right” are trying to destroy our way of life and expressing a desire to “burn this fucker down.” You won’t want to burn this record, though. The Sleights just keep getting better and better with every new release. Recommended. ![Image 44](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/strawberry.jpg) ## STRAWBERRY ALARM CLOCK – Where’s One? (Big Stir Records, https://www.bigstirrecords.com/) Holy sh*t! Yes, it’s that Strawberry Alarm Clock! The short-lived yet highly influential psychedelic rock band that formed in 1966 and released four albums in quick succession are back! Yes, they broke up back in 1971, and reunited and had some on and off again activity since the 1980's, releasing an album with a few new songs and re-recordings of some old ones (2012’s _Wake Up Where You Are_), but this is the band’s first album of all new music since 1969's _Good Morning Starshine_. And while the band may not be quite as garage-psyche as they were in their heyday, because times and music have changed, they’re still pushing the boundaries of song-craft. Well, not all new music. There are some interesting covers – but they’re new for The Strawberry Alarm Clock, not re-recordings of old songs. There’s a fascinating instrumental cover of “Day Tripper” that turns into a rocking jam with a really nice guitar tone going on. And they even tackle “Within You, Without You,” one of the Beatles’ more spacey tunes. This version takes the simple sparseness of the original and stands it on its head, twisting rhythms, bouncing the melody around, adding complexities, thickening the arrangement, though the sitar and tabla are still there. There’s a slew of entirely new songs too. We get cool, mysterious sounds in “Monsters,” blending smooth jazz-rock with angular melodic lines and even some horror-rock. There’s the freaky, experimental, psychedelic funk track, “White Light,” that’s constantly shifting. I like the funky “Blow Your Mind,” with a distinctly 70's vibe. “Live Water” is an interesting blend of soft jazz and rock. And “I’m Not the One” starts out as fairly basic 60s folk rock, but has a cool easy jazz section in the middle of the song, and at the end it mixes those two styles with a 70's psych rock jam for something pretty unique. Speaking of unique, check out “Primordial Soup,” a real “kitchen sink” sort of song that’s more experimental than traditional and has a bit of everything in it. And “Tahitian Gardens” has a commercial sound of the South Pacific, though the outro gets pretty avant garde. That’s just a handful of the baker’s dozen new tracks here. 47 years is a long time to wait between new albums! ![Image 45](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/vistablue%20so%20much.jpg) ## VISTA BLUE – So Much Music! (wearevistablue.bandcamp.com) It seems like only a few weeks ago that there was new music from Vista Blue. That’s because it was! But this two-song single is not part Mike Patton's ongoing "50 stories and 50 songs project." Patton, the force behind Vista Blue, decided to sneak in some other off-topic songs too. This single features two songs, the title track and “She Only Listens to Blue.” Both feature the Vistas’ own blend of buzzy guitars, Ramones-core meets Beach Boys melody and harmony, and tongue-in-cheek lyrics. “So Much Music” is an ode to the explosion of music to listen to via the Internet, and it’s bright and bubbly. “She Only Listens to Blue” is more frantic, as befitting a song about a relationship on the rocks over musical tastes. Also, the title can be used to describe Vista Blue’s catalog! Always enjoyable, too. * * * ![Image 46](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/diki.jpg) ## DIKI MOBS KODEN- 4-song EP (It’s Eleven Records, itselevenrecords.bandcamp.com) There’s a lot of mystery surrounding this debut EP. Google Translate tells me that the band name is Bulgarian for Wild Mobs Code. And the info sheet reads like the plot summary of a science fiction story. What I can tell you is that the four tracks on this EP are electronic, dark, and brooding, and fit well with the tenseness of that science fiction narrative. “Polar” opens things with a strong dance beat and a melody that tries hard to get its footing, with pitch changes giving the sense of time stretching and shrinking. “Diyu” has an Eastern edge, sounding like music from a time when robots take over Japan. “Guanto Nero” feels playful in comparison to the other tracks, but at times gets very eerie, you know, like a child’s doll that’s possessed by a malevolent spirit. And the last track, “Somnambulist,” is menacing and edgy, with hollow mechanical sounds like you might hear in an abandoned place where there should be no such sounds. Diki Mobs Koden provides a compelling soundscape for a bleak future.![Image 47](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/highsigh.jpg) ## HIGHSIGH – Once Bend (Joyful Noise Recordings, highsigh.bandcamp.com) HIGSIGH is a new band that features the trio of Ro(b)//ert Lundberg of JOBS, John Dieterich of Deerhoof, and Matt Mehlan of Skeletons. They’re joined by various others on various tracks, adding vocals, cornet, drums, or cello. The resulting tracks feel less like songs and more like musical compositions, less like pop and more like art. These are highly experimental songs, with complex structures and varied sonic textures. The album was created in collage fashion, with each member of the ensemble bringing in different musical fragments from other projects, and these were built upon. These fragments were traded around the group, each member reworking them into something new, and then they came back together, noting the new sonic colors and tones they each had created. The result is a fascinating sonic document, forty-five minutes of explorations in sound. Sometimes there’s breezy French pop, like in the opening track, “Don’t Crowd the Eye,” punctuated by various rhythmic jabs from percussion, from guitars, or from electronics. Other times we get science fiction hip hop mixed with the tight harmonies of 40s and 50s girl groups, like on “I Love the Room I Live In.” I like the mix of illbient rhythms and Slint-like pop of “Plastic Designed Spoonlike,” with scratchy heavily processed cello mixes, with electronics, hip drum beats, and chanted vocals. “To Grow in Lightness” is, in contrast to its title, a very dark and brooding instrumental. On the other hand, “Outcome Inevitable” is downright effervescent, though it’s incredible short. And appearing second to last, the title track is full-on avant garde, eschewing any sense of song structures or pop music in favor of creating a piece of sonic abstract art. Performance artist Laurice Anderson once created a piece for her "Home of the Brave" show that featured what she called “Difficult Listening Hour,” a fictional radio program filled with what she termed, “difficult music.” Some people may find HIGHSIGH to be difficult music. But I find that, when you immerse yourself in it, when you turn off your own thoughts and let it take control, it’s very rewarding.![Image 48](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/MISTAKES.jpg) ## THE MISTAKES – Die Laughing (Sell the Heart Records, engineerrecords.bandcamp.com) This is a new one on me. Even though The Mistakes formed way back in 2009, I was completely unfamiliar with them. Maybe I can be forgiven, since they’re located in Poole, UK. But I surely won’t forget them now, after listening to their fifth studio LP, _Die Laughing_. Their music is super-high-energy punk, with elements of street and pop varieties. They can play speedy stuff bordering on old school hardcore, and they can play stuff that’s melodic as hell, but all of it has an energetic, aggressive edge. Right from the get-go, the album opens with power and confidence in “Battle.” The anger and aggression are palpable in the growled and shouted vocals, the pummeling backing vocals, and in the high-strung guitars. There’s a song about the richest man in the world (and one of the most evil), “Elon,” which is an exciting mix of street punk and rap. We get to skank a bit with “The Pit,” a song about moshing with someone you care about. It mixes street punk and a bit of ska punk. We get some hardcore mixed with street punk on “Sons,” with an incredible rapid-fire vocal delivery and a guitar tone that emulates the sound of bagpipes. And one of the best tracks of the album is “With It and For It,” a song with a stage production quality. It’s a grand epic about creating your chosen family within the scene, people with whom you share values and good times. It’s got ska, it’s got hard rock, and it’s got rapped lyrics and it’s got a solidly punk attitude. And, of course I love the acoustic track at the end of the album, “Ready for Hell.” Acoustic is always where you get the most honest emotion from a performer, and this is no exception. “They say that time heals all wounds, but it also kills feeling,” the song tells us. It goes on to tell us that even wise men eventually become fools, that youth eventually becomes just a memory, and that we all end up alone. The song is a reflection on regrets of a life ill spent, of someone who is weary of living this life. I may not have been aware of The Mistakes before, but that mistake was mine, and one I won’t make again. * * * ![Image 49](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/damnrats.jpg) ## DAMN RATS – "Forgive & Forget" EP (Streaming) With the dissolution of longtime San Diego band Petty Saints, frontman Ciaran O’Reilly began playing solo acoustic gigs, but they didn’t quite scratch his itch to play with a full band. And so, Damn Rats was born, and "Forgive & Forget" is their debut. Petty Saints songs typically featured a mix of punk and folk, particularly with an English or Irish bent, informed by O’Reilly’s roots. But Damn Rats is a different animal. Still mixing punk with music of the people, it focuses more on Americana sounds, so there’s a hint of country twang or, more accurately, protest folk music. It’s like if Woody Guthrie and Pete Seeger electrified right along with Bob Dylan. The songs are raucous and wild, always telling stories about “broken people, bad decisions, redemption, and finding a way forward,” as the band says. For example, the first song of the EP, “Call Me Home,” is about a no-good man who smokes, drinks, gambles, and is generally a loser with no hope. He doesn’t visit his mother, he makes way too many mistakes, and is just waiting to be “called back home.” I assume this means just waiting to die. The lyrics are bleak, the music is rowdy, and O’Reilly’s vocals, with their distinct rasp, express the world weariness perfectly. I love the ballad “When You Cry,” with harmonized vocals enhancing the leads in places, and with a fantastic baritone twang in the lead guitar. It’s a song of lost or unrequited love, about seeing her with someone else, someone who is “Satan’s son.” It has the feel of something that would be at home in the _Twin Peaks_ soundtrack, sad and lonely and passionate. The title track, which closes the EP, is probably the closest to the Petty Saints’ sound, a punked up Celtic folk song about a person who finds misfortune at every turn. But I think it’s “Dead at Fifty” that’s my favorite of the EP, a song that will surely solidify O’Reilly and Damn Rats as San Diego’s version of Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band. ![Image 50](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/feeders.jpg) ## THE FEEDERS – Dark Days (thefeeders.bandcamp.com) The Feeders is not to be confused with either the punk band The Feederz or the Welsh alt-rock band Feeder. No, The Feeders are a trio formed in Chicago, initially in 2019 when Sam Vicari was invited to perform at The Taste of Chicago, an annual food festival. He happened to be scrolling through Facebook and came across a post by drummer John Perrin (NRBQ, Young Fresh Fellows), praising his 2015 solo record. Perrin told Vicari that if he ever needed a drummer to contact him. Vicari reached out and The Feeders was born. Initially recruiting Smoking Popes guitarist Eli Caterer to fill the bass spot, the trio released a debut LP. Caterer’s schedule proved unworkable, and he was amicably replaced with Alex Rackow, who appears on this sophomore album, which features what the _Chicago Reader_ called “scruffy power pop for punks who want to try their hand at ballroom dancing.” And indeed, the overall vibe is that of sentimental power pop, with tempos that aren’t too brisk. The overall feeling is one of thoughtful romanticism. The opening song, “Benevolent,” has an early Beatles-like quality and lyrics about how we don’t pay close enough attention to each other, and how that leads to misunderstanding, resentment, and aggression – and then friendships and relationships fall apart. The bouncy “Why Do We Fight,” which follows, is sort of on the same topic, questioning why there is conflict and why we feel a need to retaliate against others. The songs generally seem to cover topics such as self-deprecation, making a fool of one’s self, doing the wrong things, and so on. Like the heartbreaking ballad, “Permanent Blackout,” a song that starts with the lines,” I don’t like myself / I wish that I were someone else,” and has an allusion to suicide, with “I wish the sun would go down / A permanent blackout all over town / Wash away everything I’ve ever done / It won’t be missed by anyone.” Or the melancholy “Fruit Flies,” which has the lines, “The fruit flies, they gather around me / They don’t lie, they fly towards what’s rotten / And I’m rotten.” Not everything is so bleak in Feeders-land. “Sara, You’re My Savior” is downright bright and positive compared with the other tracks, singing about Sara, who is “one of the good ones, and then some,” who showed up when “I was dried out, strung out, but now I’m so full and green.” Sara is one of those people who make us feel good about ourselves. And don’t we all need someone like Sara? Don’t we all need albums like _Dark Days_? ![Image 51](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/jimmy%20c.jpg) ## THE JIMMY C – Pretending to Be a Person (Kool Kat Musik) Who is The Jimmy C, you ask? It’s none other than Jamie Coghill, a multi-instrumentalist singer-songwriter from Australia, who also is a member of Lava Fangs. He’s been releasing solo material under the Jimmy C moniker since 2005 as a way to showcase his home recordings. And now, more than two decades and several EPs and LPs later, he’s "Pretending to be a Person."" Or at least that’s the title of his latest record, his second album for Kool Kat Musik. His music tends toward power pop, classic rock, blues and folk rock, sometimes blending these styles together. He’s essentially a one-man band, playing all the instruments himself, multi-tracking vocals and harmonizing with himself, and doing all the recording. It’s an amazing feat, because all of the instruments and singing are done really well, the singing and harmonizing are pitch perfect, and the recording quality is aces. We get folk rock tunes with acoustic guitars blending in with electric on songs like “All I Want Is for the Summer to Be Here,” “Are You Angry,” or “They Put on a Show.” “Near the Painting of the Girl by the Sea,” with strings and acoustic guitars, is like an aural painting with a lush soundscape. We get breezy, driving rockers like “Fewer than Everyone” (one of my faves of the LP,) or “Waiting for You."" And we get bouncy AM pop tunes like “You’re Never Alone.” The title track occurs about two thirds of the way through the album, and is a solemn yet tense instrumental. Although the album isn’t going to set the world on fire, the variety and pleasant performances provide something for everyone. ![Image 52](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/man%20mountain.jpg) ## MAN MOUNTAIN – Threads of Another Life (Spartan Records, spartanrecords.com) Formed nearly a decade and a half ago, Man Mountain keep the flames of post-rock burning. It’s been eight long years since their previous LP, _Infinity Mirror_, and it finds the band in fine, pensive form. On _Threads of Another Life_, they present seven expansive instrumental tracks that are dreamy and emotive. These songs express a huge range, from quiet, thoughtful moments to enormous peaks of ecstasy. From the first moment of the first piece, you’re immersed in another world, enveloped in new sonic realities, and you’re taken on a journey. Words become unnecessary, as the music tells you everything you need to know. We meander for nearly forty minutes across seven tracks, experiencing the brightness of oblivion on “Bright Oblivion,” with shiny guitars that express occasional aggression, but mostly sparkle. Or the serenity of a “Halcyon Dream,” with a nostalgic pastoral feeling to it. But, as in life, there are sad moments, as well as pleasant ones. Grief and loss are explored in the somber, “Absence/Descent.” It’s got a repeating drum riff pulled way back in the mix, representing something or someone we remember, but is gone from our lives. Guitars and bass solemnly swirl around us, as if trying to find meaning in it, and we sometimes hear the anger that comes with loss, as the music reaches crescendos of guitars. Man Mountain may leave long gaps of time between releases, but what they lack in quantity they make up for in quality. ![Image 53](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/okaylindon.jpg) ## OKAY LINDON (Lost In Ohio, lostinohio.com) What’s the deal with bands taking several years between albums? In the case of Okay Lindon, it’s been 14 years since their last LP. I mean, there were albums in in 2016 and 2019, but those didn’t feature the band’s full complement. The band members are no longer all located close together, so getting together to practice or record is difficult. Singer Dustin Smith proposed they get together once a month, bring a mostly-completed song, and see what happens. They met in drummer Chuck Smith’s basement, and within a couple of months, they could see this experiment was working. The result of these sessions formed the basis of their new self-titled LP, and that produced melodic indie rock that’s hazy and relaxed. It sounds more like a bunch of friends making music together for fun than a band trying to impress anyone. I love the opening track, “Pinto vs. Pinto,” a gauzy song about a tragic figure who is self-defeating. I love the lush guitar tone, with distorted chords chiming out like broken church bells. The roots of the song were in a challenge to take a page from a book and write about the contents of that page. In this case, it was the story of Stanley Pinto, who got tangled in the ropes entering a wrestling ring, and was counted out before the match even started. It’s a metaphor for the thing we do to ourselves that prevent our own success. I also like the hypnotic quality of the guitar riffs on “Bootstrap Lovers,” the easy jazzy vibe of “Casual Fridays,” and the mysterious tone of “On Our Way to Avalon.” There are eight songs in total, just under 30 minutes of music, and none of it feels rushed or overdone. ![Image 54](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/SAR%20FRONT.jpg) ## THE SOMETHING AIN’T RIGHTS – Rotten in the Brain (Hovercraft Records, www.hovercraftrecords.com) The Something Ain’t Rights hail from Astoria, Oregon, site of filming for _The Goonies_. So, right off the bat, you know something’s going to be wrong in the head here, in the best way possible. And that’s the case. _Rotten in the Brain_ is one of the most disjointed albums I’ve heard in a long time, but also one of the most creative and original. The band, in its current state, was formed when Mike Vasquez, owner and chief engineer at Austin, Texas’ Sweatbox Studio, relocated to Astoria. He initiated an earlier iteration in Austin, but after his big move, he proceeded to recruit drummer Carrie Beveridge, bassist Alpha Rasmussen, and guitarist Dan McClure, and they chose the most appropriate name they could, because... well, something ain’t right! It’s very wrong, but in all the right ways! This debut mini-LP (nine songs in about 20 minutes) covers the gamut from country to jazz to post punk and everything in between. They cite influences as diverse as X, The Minutemen, Pere Ubu, The Gun Club, and Wire, and they sound like all of them and none of them. They are themselves, they are unique. As soon as you think you know what kind of band they are, they change things up on you. The mini-LP opens with the title track, a twisted rockin’ down home country tune that twangs as hard as it rocks. But then we get “Plymouths of Fury,” a dissonant angular jazz-rock tune about driving a Plymouth Fury, with its V-8 and plenty of room, because “we’re in a hurry” and “there gonna be no fascists when we’re done when we’re through.” There’s 80's post punk in “Melt Melt,” and we jump right back to jazzy swing with “Gas Station Angel,” an ode to a woman who works the night shift at the gas station and takes no shit. The band takes their name from the state of the world, because something ain’t right in the world today. One of those things is described in “Spineless Men in Masks,” a militaristic post punk track about Donald Trump’s ICE. It declares that “We won’t sit on the sidelines as these fucks keep crossing all the red lines” and “bringing on the end times of democracy.” Through all these different sounds, there’s something very right about The Something Ain’t Rights. The songs vary, and you can’t pin them down to a genre, but the band is always recognizable. That’s the mark of genius. * * * ![Image 55](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/bandaal9.jpg) ## BANDA AL9 – Hey! Hey! We’re Banda AL9! (Wicked Cool Records, www.wickedcoolrecords.com) Brazilian pop rock band Banda AL9 is led by a pair of brothers, Matheus and Thiago Khouri. They broke into public consciousness with a series of viral TikTok videos that reached a staggering 12 million views and rising. This caught the attention of Steven Van Zandt, who played their music on his Little Steven’s Underground Garage program and signed them to his record label. Though they’ve released a series of digital singles and digital albums over the years, this album serves as their introduction to the wider world outside of social media algorithms and the like. It collects many of the fan favorites from those digital releases, and includes some brand new tracks as well. Banda AL9 take their inspiration from American music of the 1960's, playing sunny pop music that channels early Beatles and Beach Boys sounds. It’s fun, good-time music that harkens back to much simpler times. Beatles inspired songs include “She Calls Me Love, which opens the album, as well as the jangly “She Can Do It All.” And “Love Bug” mixes Chuck Berry rock 'n' roll with Beatles-era ,&B sounding like the classic “Birthday, from Tth White Album. The band leans into their Beach Boys influence in songs like “American Girl,” which will transport you to a Southern California beach in the 1960s' quicker than the TARDIS. And there are songs that, while reimagining the 60s' sound, are wholly the band’s own style. One such song is “California,” with the warmth of an electric organ, gorgeous vocal harmonies, and solid 60s' pop hooks. And I enjoy “Indigo Skye,” with its 60s' harpsichord jangle and 70s' guitar riffs. But I think my favorite of the album is “The Only One,” with a unique sound that blends all of the influences together. If you’re a fan of 60's retro pop, you’re gonna love this. ![Image 56](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/bigcircle.jpg) ## BIG CIRCLE (bigcirclemusic.bandcamp.com) You might think a new recording by a “supergroup” featuring indie and punk rock legends Glenn Mercer (Feelies), Mike Watt (Minutemen, fIREHOUSE), Dave Weckerman (Feelies), and Dan Francia (Speed the Plough) would be exciting and dynamic. You might be wrong. This debut four-song EP is all-instrumentals and it somewhat plods along with little in the way of dynamic or melodic variation. The first track, in particular, feels lazy and tired. “Flipped Over” has the sound of a classic rock band practicing covers more than a supergroup of indie rockers creating something new. The pace just drags, and the guitar riffs sound phoned in. While three of the four recorded together in New Jersey and Watt recorded his bass part in his West Coast studio, and though the bass tone sounds delicious, the bass lines often sound tentative and meandering. “Calling All Gods” is a little better, with spacey sounding keyboards and throbbing guitars and bass, but it does sound more like a jam on a theme than a song of any kind. It has the same lack of dynamic variation and also drags too much, tempo-wise. “Exit Plan” is a mid-tempo edgy jam more than a song, and “Signs Along the Way” is a soft, smooth ballad. The tracks sound more improvised than planned, too. I love Watt, I love The Feelies, and I love Speed the Plough. This EP was a disappointment. Apparently they plan to include vocals when they release their debut LP, so hopefully that will be better than these tentative experiments. ![Image 57](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/jerkazoid.jpg) ## JERKAZOID – Earth In Reverse (jerkazoid.bandcamp.com) I’m not quite sure how long ago it was that Jerkazoid formed as a band, but if Google is to be believed, it was in 2019. And it’s taken the Portland, Oregon trio until now to start releasing music. But we won’t hold that against them, because it was worth the wait. They play fun Fest-style pop punk, sometimes with speedy skate punk elements, sometimes with a bit of West Coast emo angst mixed in, but always with solid power, a sharp edge, and bouncy jangly melodies. The musicianship is top notch, and the arrangements are thoughtful. Sure, there are elements of humor here and there (and in the band name), but there’s also a clear sincerity in these songs, and passion in the vocals. It’s hard to pigeonhole Jerkazoid too much. The album opener, “Runaway,” is mostly a great pop punk song with ardent vocals and an unconventional melody, and I really like how the song, toward the end, has a bridge where the music slows and smooths and gets really introspective, and then gets broadly emo. But only a couple tracks later, “Six Minutes Away” uses the speed of skate punk and the power of emo to craft the song. Sometimes we get exactly what we expect, like with “King of the Middle of Nowhere,” which channels the band’s inner Blink-182. And Jerkazoid can go dark, too; “Somebody Kill ‘Em (Pretty Please)” is aggressively dark melodic punk. But I love the harmonies of “Cops Don’t Rock.” The melodic line and chord progressions are unusual for a pop punk song, and it’s gorgeous. The guitars are appropriately and aggressively noisy, but the vocals are beautifully smooth. It’s a wonderful contrast. And after releasing all that punk energy throughout the album, the band closes with a pretty acoustic song, “No Comfort.” Not a lot of bands are still making pop punk quite like this anymore. Better yet, no one is making pop punk that sounds this fresh and vital. ![Image 58](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/monogroove.jpg) ## MONOGROOVE – Anthology (Kool Kat Musik, www.koolkatmusik.com) Monogroove is a retro-pop band from the far northern California coastal town of Crescent City. They’ve been kicking around playing their brand of sunny music since the 1990's. Over the past few decades of their career, they’ve released some seven LP's. But there’s more to that story! There are songs recorded in a tiny apartment. There are demos that were never released, save to a handful of people on cassettes sold at shows. And they’re all here, on this new collection of unreleased songs that span the band’s career, including three brand new songs just recorded for this anthology. The band’s light 60's style pop music with three-part harmonies brings to mind a cross between The Beatles and the Beach Boys. And for decades old recordings that were done at home or on the cheap, the sound quality is pretty good. I can only imagine the effort that went into remastering these tracks. One of the newly recorded tracks is the opener, “Back to School,” and it has a glam-tinged power pop vibe, reminding me of a lighter version of Cheap Trick. Another is “Autopilot,” which appears midway through, and the closer, “Betty Can’t Come,” is the third brand new one. These two are a couple of the most raucous tracks of the collection, a little more energetic and emphatic, but still with a retro-power/sunshine pop sound. “Spanish Dancer” is unique, with a Latin-pop flair, complete with trumpet and flamenco guitar in the arrangement, giving it a Mexican cinematic quality. Another song that’s different from the others is “Stones of Paris, which has a soulful R&B quality to it, though lightened a bit by folk pop. And “Let Me Come” has an interesting mix of ska rhythm and country swagger! “Punk.com” has a soulful sound, too, sans punk edge. “Dusk Until Dawn” has more of a 60's folk rock and sunshine pop sound, kind of like The Mamas and the Papas. And speaking of folk rock, “Little America” has the feel of a style that was popular in the 60's, making a song sound both modern and traditional at the same time. So does “No One Here,” for that matter, complete with acoustic guitars and strings. And one of my favorite tracks is “Rain Parade,” a Beatles-esque track recorded back in 1998. It features super jangly guitars and intense vocal harmonies, with a droning undercurrent, sort of like the music the Fab Four started doing after their visit to India. Speaking of The Beatles, there’s a song here called “Sexy Never Knows,” which is a rearrangement of “Tomorrow Never Knows” from _Revolver_, heavier on the sunshine pop and lighter on the eastern mysticism. All in all, there are twenty tracks here and just over an hour of music. If you’re a fan of retro sunshine pop, it’s an interesting document. ![Image 59](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/cryforhelp.jpg) ## GLENN MORROW’S CRY FOR HELP – Our Final Album Vol. 1 (Bar/None Records, www.bar-none.com) Earlier this year, longtime proprietor of the storied Bar/None Records, Glenn Morrow, turned a page as he handed over the label's reins to Emmy Black. Thus, in the label’s 40th anniversary year, Morrow finds himself with some time on his hands, and what better way to use that time than to go back to making music? Morrow, of course, performed with the rock band The Individuals in the 1970's, and was in the band ‘a,’ the first band to play at Maxwell’s, the famous home of indie music in Hoboken, New Jersey. Morrow and his friends - Mike Rosenberg, Ric Sherman, and Ron Metz - formed Glenn Morrow’s Cry for Help in 2015, playing their first show at the Hoboken Arts & Music Festival in September of that year. Albums followed in 2017 and 2020, but no new recorded output has issued forth – until now. And I’m guessing the album title, like many of the lyrics in his songs, is a tongue-in-cheek joke (of course, a final album isn’t final if there are further volumes to follow). The music on this album blends indie rock, power pop, classic rock, bluesy riffs, and pretty much anything else that sounds good. And the band does it all without getting overly heavy or complicated; this is understated stuff, lighter and more relaxed than you might imagine. And it’s quite varied. I like the tentative nature of “Autumn Leaves,” which is not the classic popularized by Nat King Cole and others. It’s got a stripped-back arrangement, but it, too, is wistful and melancholy, ruminating on the transitory nature of our lives. It’s a majestic, thoughtful song. The tone changes completely with “Beatle Bones,” a song that channels classic 60's and 70's rock and soul, sounding like a lost Rolling Stones tune, but also featuring some guitar licks that sound like they could have come from a Beatles record. And then things change drastically again with the lounge-like love song, “Boom Boom.” There’s the very cinematic and romantic “In Love With Love,” and the jangly “Sweater Weather.” “Stop Your Crying” is a real stand-out of the album, very different from all of the other songs. It’s subtle and it’s very moving, an admonition to someone to stop the self-pity and to realize they are loved and that they can achieve what they need and want out of life. There’s a slow steady pulse in the percussion and gravitas in the instrumentals, and it slowly grows in intensity. It’s the kind of song I can’t stop listening to. The album closer, “Begin Again,” may be somewhat autobiographical for Morrow, as he turns that page in his life, and sings a song about deciding that life needs a change, even as the lyrics seem to reminisce about the past. It’s interesting that this album is coming out so closely on the heels of a new LP from Graham Parker & the Goldtops, because there are certainly parallels. They both have been making music for decades and both play music that has many similarities. And it’s nice listening to music made by an adult for a change. ![Image 60](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/motorcycle.jpg) ## MOTORCYCLE – Relive It (Dandy Boy Records, dandyboyrecords.bandcamp.com) They’re called Sacramento’s premiere middle-aged teen pop band, and it’s hilariously accurate! On their debut LP, Motorcycle mostly sounds like gritty New Wave, with big buzzy synths and bright female vocals, kind of like The Human League. A perfect example of this is “Down That Road,” the lead-off song. “Spinning Out of Control,” too, has big buzzy synths and a definite new wave vibe, but this time it’s those dreamy new wave ballads they’re emulating. “Here but not Here” is another, this time with a melancholy sound. The goth punks who also like a bit of pop are gonna go crazy for this one. But Motorcyle has a variety of sonic textures to offer too. The title track leans harder into Pop Punk, with over-the-top vocals that are right out of the PUP songbook, but also blend in those sparkling New Wave synths. “Don’t Even Try” and “All In My Head” have a cool nerdy Pop Punk sound. And “Friday the 13th “ is big and grand, mixing the new wave and pop punk vibes with a Broadway show tune aesthetic. Though their songs bring up memories of other bands, no one else I can think of is playing anything that sounds quite like this. Cool stuff. ![Image 61](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/tiger%20bear%20wolf.jpg) ## TIGER BEAR WOLF (Ernest Jenning Record Co., www.ernestjenning.com) Tiger Bear Wolf, from North Carolina, formed in 2002 and proceeded to release two albums: _Tiger_ in 2003, and a self-titled LP in 2005. Tracks for a third LP were laid down in 2009, but the project was never released. Time intervened, people drifted away, and due to hardware failures, the tracks were thought to be lost forever. But in 2015, through the use of specialized software and the intervention of a musical savior, the tracks were almost fully recovered. And over the past decade, they've been lovingly restored, mixed, and mastered to perfection, and we now have the lost third LP, mysteriously also self-titled. Tiger Bear Wolf is typically described as a “Post-Hardcore” band. Maybe because in the 2000's, bands were either categorized as post-hardcore, Pop Punk, or Emo, and they’re definitely not Emo or Pop Punk. But Tiger Bear Wolf are not really Post-Hardcore either. They blend a variety of styles together to create something outside these genre categories. Sure, I hear elements of Post-Hardcore, but the music isn’t quite as hard and aggressive as genre heroes like Refused or Quicksand. I hear elements of Southern Rock, too, but they aren’t overly twangy like The Allman Brothers, Molly Hatchet, or The Black Crowes. There are definite tinges of Post-Rock and Math Rock, which were also popular genres in the 90's and 2000's. This is more like alternative/indie rock with other touches mixed in than straight up Post-Hardcore. Listening to the opening track, “Bronco Town, USA,” for example, you can definitely hear some down-home Southern sounds, but it’s not the dominant element of the music. This one is a heavy slow burner of a song with a dusty desert sound, mixed with some grunge and some jazzy breaks, along with the hints of twang. It’s a fascinating mélange of stuff that you think wouldn’t necessarily blend well together, but it ends up being pretty tasty. Which is an apt description of the album as a whole. ![Image 62](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/woodenhorse.jpg) ## VISTA BLUE – "Wooden Horse" (wearevistablue.bandcamp.com) Vista Blue is the project of one Mike Patton, also known for his stint in The Loblaws. Vista Blue is both his solo project and a full band, depending on the mood and the circumstances. But Vista Blue’s releases always have a theme, whether it be opening day of baseball, a seasonal change, a holiday, or whatever else strike’s Patton’s fancy. In the case of this latest single, “Wooden Horse,” the impetus is the release of the movie _The Odyssey._ The ancient, epic tale recounts the story of Odysseus (also known as Ulysses) and his men as they travel home from The Trojan War, which they famously won through the deception of a giant wooden horse. This song marks a distinct change for Vista Blue, who famously rely primarily on bold buzzy guitars for their instrumentals. Here the focus is on guitar, bass, and drums, and though the guitar tone is appropriately gritty, they also have the beauty of strings (probably synthetic), giving the song the epic quality it deserves. The song picks up when are heroes have been gone from home for so many years they can’t even remember how long it’s been. And their only desire is to make it home to their loves. It’s classic Vista Blue, in one sense, but it’s so much more because of the gorgeous arrangement. It’s also the introduction to a new phase for Vista Blue: Patton says he plans to release 50 songs based on 50 stories or books he likes. They will be collected together next spring, and Homer’s _The Odyssey_ is the first. Whether you plan to go see the film or not, you should do yourself a favor and check out “Wooden Horse.” ![Image 63](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/gordon%20withers%20single.jpg) ## GORDON WITHERS – "Never Meant" b/w "Calba’s Last" (sweet-cheetah-records.com) Gordon Withers is the rock and roll cellist. He’s the spiritual successor to the late Tom Cora and often performs with J Robbins, Zach Barocas’ New Freedom Sound, and is part of the collective We All Inherit the Moon. He plays Post Punk, Post-Hardcore, and modern Classical styles. And he’s released solo material as well, including his well-regarded cover albums of songs by Jawbox and Jawbreaker. He’s teaming up with Sweet Cheetah Records for their “Covers for a Cause” series, and 100% of proceeds from the sale of this single will be donated to the Southern Poverty Law Center. And if that’s not enough incentive to pick this up, well, do it for the music. The A-side is a cover of American Football’s “Never Meant,” a classically pensive Midwest Emo song from their debut LP. In place of the lush jangly guitars, Withers’ cello is multi-tracked to weave a glorious sonic tapestry. Replacing the wistful vocals is the glorious singing of his cello. He creates a pastoral landscape that I want to get lost in. The B-side, “Calba’s Last,” is a cover from Ethel Meserve, an underrated emo band from the 1990's. Withers’ version of the song is suitably melancholic, but also stately and grand, giving the sense of faded glory yet also of perseverance. Both songs are gorgeous, and even if this wasn’t a benefit for a good cause, I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend it. * * * ![Image 64](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/a100s.jpg) ## A-100S – Rude and Lovely (Pirates Press Records, a100sband.bandcamp.com) The unlikeliest of “super-groups,” reggae/rock-steady/ska band A-100s were created by Matt Hensely (accordionist for Celtic punks Flogging Molly) and Sean Wheeler (vocalist of garage punkabilly and desert rock band Throw Rag). Both artists have long had a love for Jamaican music, and Hensley even played guitar and keyboards in the 90's ska band Spy Kids, several members of whom actively contribute to A-100s recordings and performances. The music on this debut LP could primarily be categorized as Rock-steady, too slow to qualify as ska and too brisk to be considered Reggae. There’s also a deep Soul and R&B influence in a lot of the tracks, most notably on the title track that opens the LP. Of the title, Wheeler explains he was driving through Mexico City, when he saw a beauty salon with a beautifully hand-painted sign that said, “Rude and Lovely.” Thinking it a perfect phrase to describe the music they had started making together, he excitedly called Hensley, and the title stuck. The song features the warmth of an organ, a nice loping pace, clean-toned guitars, and soulful backing vocals. It’s sheer joy. Another uplifting track is “Too Rad to Be Sad,” a song that reminds us to keep our heads up, that we are loved, we are all we need, and we should remain positive in the face of adversity and naysayers. “Stand back, deep breath, rewind your day,” the song exhorts. “Were you acting unruly? Did you mind slip away?” it asks, before explaining that “these blues, they feel like forever, but trust me, they’re just passing through.” Some songs are a little more soulful and funkier than others, like “Number One,” a song with a Rock-steady beat and bass guitar, but with funky saxophones, twangy guitar riffs, and deeply soulful lead vocals. And “Soul Rumble” is aptly named, as it’s more 70's R&B and Soul than anything else, and is a stand-out track of the album. I love the trumpets and trombones in the arrangement, and the dark urban tone of the song. Some of the songs have different vibes, too. “Luxury Nights” is a curiously cool blend of Reggae music and surf guitars, and the passionate lead vocals are reminiscent of a Tom Waits’ growl. And there’s a hint of European folk in “Wires,” mostly from the accordion riffs and the melodic lines. The A-100s’ debut LP is a pleasant surprise, easy to listen to. ![Image 65](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/amonglegends2.jpg) ## AMONG LEGENDS – Lose My Grip (amonglegends519.bandcamp.com) It’s been a few years since I reviewed Among Legends’ debut LP, _Take Good Care._ When I reviewed that LP four years ago, I noted that these Canadian punks lived in the space between melodic hardcore, skate rock, and pop punk. I commented that the songs were catchy enough, but often felt too safe and middle of the road. Their sophomore LP, _Lose My Grip_, is a definite step up - more like several steps up. While still catchy and poppy, the band has honed the melodic punk tendencies to a sharpened edge. The band is more aggressive, more powerful, and tighter than ever. That the band is a mere trio (Tyler Boles, Guitar; Mitchell Buchanan, bass, vocals; Sara Fellin, drums, vocals) is amazing because they have an enormous sound. On a scale of one to 10, the album starts at an 11 and never lets up. “H/A/C/K” is an edgy post-hardcore tune that immediately changed my preconceptions of what this album would be like. There was more raw aggression and power than I was expecting. And “Sound the Alarm” is speedy crunchy hardcore with solid melody and amazing harmonized vocals. Not since Pears have I heard a band so effectively meld pop punk and gritty hardcore. Things get cranked up another notch with “Go On,” with an even brisker tempo and mind-blowing fast-paced harmonized vocals. Some of the tracks are both poppy punk and emotionally charged, like “Back Again,” with big broad vocals that soar. And “Familiar Fictions” is the stand-out of the album, with a different sound than anything else on the LP. It’s post-hardcore, it’s indie rock, it’s emo, and it’s beautiful. I particularly like how, near the end of the song, things get dreamy in the instrumentals and the vocals bounce back and forth between Buchanan and Fellin. And some tracks lean back on the Bad Religion sort of sound, like “Open Wide,” though toward the end of the song there’s an intense youth crew hardcore breakdown. Another favorite is “Band Dudes Fuck Off,” which features guest vocals by Laura DeRocchis. It’s a rocking tune about the prevalence in the scene of “band dudes” who sexually harass women at shows, sometimes going so far as to not take no for an answer. The anger and mocking tone are strong, and DeRocchis’ singing is intensely ireful. There’s the old saw about a band’s sophomore slump, where the second LP doesn’t live up to the promise of the first. I’d say _Among Legends_ has turned that on its head, and _Lose My Grip_ exceeds all expectations. Recommended! ![Image 66](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/hackedpicciotto.jpg) ## HACKEDEPICCIOTTO – Lichtung (hackedepicciotto.bandcamp.com) A portmanteau of the names of the two principles, Hackedepicciotto is Alexander Hacke, formerly of Einstürsende Newbauten, and visual artist Danielle de Picciotto. As might be expected, their music eschews traditional rock and roll structures for a more avant garde sound, filled with atmospheric electronics, strings, hurdy gurdies, and bowed or throbbing bass. The music is often dark and brooding, sometimes light and romantic, always filled with mystery. There are elements of classical music, experimental, and folk in their songs, and for the first time with this new album, the songs are entirely sung in German (Hacke is from Germany, while de Picciotto is an American who has lived in Germany for decades). The album title, _Lichtung_, means “Clearing,” and was chosen when the pair decided to end their roaming and settle down in one place. They selected a home on the distant outskirts of Berlin, among nature and open fields. The clearing of the title refers to a place where you can suddenly see the light after roaming through a thick, dark forest. Not only does it refer to the end of their own roaming, but it’s also a prayer for hope for light in the increasing darkness of the world. The eight tracks on _Lichtung_ are mostly extended pieces, often in the range of six to eight minutes long, with only a few in the three minute range. This gives Hackedepicciotto the room for these compositions to breathe and live – and that’s what they do. They’re like living organisms that grow and change. The title track opens the album, featuring electronics, sound effects, throbbing bass, violins, and vibraphone. You can hear the nature of the titular clearing, the animals and the insects, and you can hear the calm and beauty of the setting and the warmth of the sun. “Vogelfrei” is next, and the title translates to “Outlawed.” As such, this is a darker piece, with grittier vocals, and mysteriously thrumming ambience. “Wiederbelebung,” or “Resuscitation,” has a militaristic rhythm, while “Erntedank” (which is a harvest festival or Thanksgiving), has a mechanical feel, yet is also pastoral, giving the feeling of harvesting machines reaping the bounty of nature. “Zeitenwende” (“Turning Point”) has a stately and hopeful sound, perhaps the brightest and most optimistic piece of the album. “Draussen” (“Outside”) sounds like the soundtrack to a spy thriller, very cinematic, mysterious, and intriguing. “Einig” (“In Agreement”) is the penultimate track, and has the air of a sonic resolution, while in the closing song, “Der Marschall” (“The Marshal,” referring to a military commander), you can feel the weariness from carrying the weight of the world and holding the fate of millions. It’s solemn and melancholy, the chimes tolling for the dead. The entirety of the album is a tour de force, an amazing achievement that, while very different from most of the music we cover here in Jersey Beat, is wonderful to listen to. ![Image 67](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/ryanhamilton2.jpg) ## RYAN HAMILTON – Haunted by American Dreams (Wicked Cool Records, www.wickedcoolrecords.com) What is the “American Dream?” To some it’s a family in a home with a white picket fence. To others it’s a well-paying job with the respect and material success that can bring. And to others it’s as simple as being able to do better than your parents. But to most people in America today, the American Dream has become elusive, It’s a broken promise, a cruel hoax, something we’re told we should strive for, but like Charlie Brown’s football, it’s snatched away anytime we get close. And that’s the theme that weaves through this new album from singer-songwriter and radio/podcast personality Ryan Hamilton. Hamilton is living his own version of the American Dream, having played SXSW in 2010 and subsequently enjoying a modicum of success in the world of indie music, including signing to Little Steven Van Zandt’s Wicked Cool Records. Hamilton’s latest LP, _Haunted by American Dreams_, features his own blend of power pop, indie rock, and Americana. His songs have a thoughtful, introspective, and story-telling quality, with songs about the illusion and elusion of happiness in modern America, whether that be love, material comforts, or spiritual contentment. Most songs are solidly in the power pop and rock and roll category, like “Dreaming Screaming,” a song about picking all the wrong people to get into relationships with. Or the title track, which has slightly twangy rock and roll verses and an indie rock chorus, and lyrics about selfishly chasing desire without regard to the feelings of others. Then there’s “Weed and Wine,” an ode to using substances to cope with hard times and disappointments. I said this when I reviewed an earlier album from Hamilton, Haunted by the Holy Ghost: This LP isn’t going to shake the world, but it’s a solid listen if you enjoy power pop and rock. ![Image 68](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/jamie%20james.jpg) ## JAMIE JAMES – Stepping Back 2004 (Oglio Entertainment, www.oglio.com) Jamie James is a long-time Los Angeles musician best known as the frontman of rockabilly trio The Kingbees, as well as his work with Harry Dean Stanton and Dennis Quaid & the Sharks. And this year, Oglio Entertainment has been digging into the archives for some special career retrospective releases under the _Steppin’ Back_ moniker. I love the hushed tone of “Impossible Love,” a pure folk singer-songwriter tour de force. And “Mother Earth (She Waits for You)” features some cool harmonica work, an Americana vibe and a solid power pop melody. And the closing track, “Find Your Faith,” nay be the best of the album, with a solemn spiritual quality. Some of the tracks lean harder toward folk vibes, while others feature a down-home Americana sound. They’re all lighter fare, mostly with a sense of joy, rather than heavy emotional material. It makes for a pleasant listen. ![Image 69](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/kiraroessler.jpg) ## KIRA ROESSLER – Enigma (Org Music, kiraroessler.bandcamp.com) Kira Roessler, of course, is the legendary bassist for an important period in the existence of Black Flag, as well as the bass-driven group dos with another legendary bassist, Mike Watt. _Enigma_ is Roessler’s second solo LP, and it sees her collaborating with her brother, Paul Roessler, who produced the LP, and with Petra Haden, daughter of legendary jazz bassist Charlie Haden. Petra contributes backing vocals to this stripped back LP, that features a trio of bass, piano, and drums, along with the Roessler’s distinctive vocals.
