The vibe reminds me of a particular period of Lydia Lunch’s career, when she, too, explored jazz-influenced music with her 1980 LP, _Queen of Siam._ I also will point out the potential for influence from her dos partner, Watt, who has dabbled quite a bit in avant garde jazz as a member of MSSV. As can be expected, the bass takes the forefront here, with piano providing texture more than melody. Roessler’s dry, matter-of-fact vocal delivery is a contrast to Haden’s sensuous backing vocals. The opening track, “Peas,” is a gorgeously sultry torch song that also features guitar and electric organ, and lyrics that use foods as similes for aspects of a romantic relationship. “You Will Feel My Pain,” too, is a ballad, but with more of an edge to it, expressing hurt, both physical and emotional. And though the pace of all of the tracks is very relaxed and laid-back, some of them have a bit of a hop to them. “How Could You” is one of those, with a definite spring in its step. And “Jim” is downright funky. I like the easy bounce of “Collapse,” a quirky song about how everything will eventually break down, and I think it refers not just to machines, but also to political and social entities, such as empires and governments. And “Drinking and Driving” is a jumping cautionary tale of addiction and its severe consequences. _Enigma_ is an interesting document, and another example of important figures in punk stretching the boundaries of their music. It’s a nice listen, but I do wish there was a little more variation in textures among the songs. ![Image 70](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/sundayclub.jpg) ## SUNDAYCLUB (Paper Bag Records, paperbagrecords.com) Winnipeg may best be known as the home of the NHL’s Winnipeg Jets, but the South Central Canadian city is also home to a thriving music scene. It is the birthplace of major performers such as The Guess Who, Neil Young, The Crash Test Dummies, and Bachman-Turner Overdrive. And it’s also the home of a bustling indie scene. One of these bands is sundayclub, the duo of vocalist Courtney Carmichael and multi-instrumentalist Nikki St. Pierre. Forming in 2019, after meeting while attending university, they’re finally releasing their debut LP. And if you look up “dream pop” in the dictionary, you’ll find a photo of the two of them, along with a link to listen to their music. The tracks on this LP are hazy and reverb-drenched, filled with bright pop melodies, melancholy instrumentals, and introspective vocals. Listening to songs like “Blue Wave,” you could be listening to major pop artists, except the arrangement here is much more complex than arena bubblegum pop, much more sweeping and epic in sound. Carmichael’s vocals are gorgeous, silky smooth, and the instrumentals are lush and, well dreamy. “Blue Wave” soars uncontrollably, and is a real stand-out. “Camera Shy,” too, has a melody worthy of any of a number of top pop artists of today. But it’s the more atmospheric songs that I like best. Songs like “Tune In,” which opens the album, are simply otherworldly. And “Sober” is really like something out of a dream, light and ethereal. sundayclub’s debut LP is lovely stuff. ![Image 71](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/twinbloom.jpg) ## TWIN BLOOM (Dandy Boy Records, twinbloom.bandcamp.com) Most dream pop is lush, thick, and melancholy, but Oakland’s Twin Bloom mixes a sparer 80's aesthetic into its brand of dream pop, giving it a slightly brighter and more upbeat feel. It’s not like this record is sparkly sunshine stuff; compared to, say, typical indie pop, it’s thick and lush and a bit morose. But by dream pop standards, this is downright jangly and happy. It’s nice stuff, particularly “Magazine Dreams,” a song that could have been a radio hit in 1983. I just wish the recording quality was a little better. It’s like listening to a bedroom demo, with compressed and clipped frequency bands and more noise than I’d like. * * * ![Image 72](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/fuses.jpg) ## FUSES – Sawdust in the Transmission (Having Fun Records, bandetfuses.bandcamp.com) Fuses is a trans-Atlantic duo featuring drummer/bassist Moa-Linn Rosenlöf (from Gothenburg, Sweden) and Guitarist Craig Fahner (from Toronto and New York). The closing track, “Bakom Molnen,” even though it also has a slow pace, is a great slow burner, with some bluesy guitar licks. Sawdust in the Transmission is a nice hazy, lazy debut for fans of relaxed folk rock and Americana. ![Image 73](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/julez.jpg) ## JULEZ AND THE ROLLERZ – Dirty Little Rock ‘n’ Roller (Lolipop Records, julezandtherollerz.bandcamp.com) Julez and the Rollerz is the project of Jules Batterman, an LA musician that sings and plays guitar on this debut LP, along with friends Shea Carothers (keyboards, vocals), Morgun Payge (bass, vocals), and Sarah Park (AKA Spark, drums). The band plays a particularly Los Angeles brand of power pop that’s polished with glam and glitz, ready-made for clubbing in Hollywood. Mixing the rock 'n' roll grit of progenitors The Runaways (Joan Jett is even a stated inspiration) with 70's glam rock and 80's new wave kitsch (thanks to the atmospheric synths,) Julez and the Rollerz offer up nearly 30 minutes of retro-rock good-time party music that will transport you back to a previous generation, while still sounding rooted in today’s aesthetic. The music is poppy without sounding sappy and silly, with just enough rock and roll power. The songs are energetic and upbeat, designed to take your mind off the troubles of the world instead of constantly reminding you of them. I like the new wave-inspired, angular riffs in “Phaser,” and I enjoy the jazzy rhythms of “Call Me Up.” “Hot Take” is the song that gives the album its title, with self-aware references to “LA musicians posturing as reincarnated 70's rock stars” and tongue-in-cheek pokes at the ego that goes along with that persona. Julez and the Rollerz’ earlier material (they’ve previously released an EP and some singles) focused more on grittier garage rock like that, along with lilting indie-pop, and I think there’s more personality in those songs than most of what’s on the LP. While some of the songs are pretty good, I think they’re playing it too safe with the polish on this LP. ![Image 74](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/mantocharen.jpg) ## MANTAROCHEN – "Wellness Ward" EP (It’s Eleven Records, itselevenrecords.bandcamp.com) Leipzig, Germany’s Mantarochen has released a slew of singles, an EP, and an LP in their short existence. JUGGERNAUT – "Firecracker (Fourth of July)" (Nickel Eye Records, jrjuggernaut.bandcamp.com) Bridging the gap between last year’s critically praised LP, _Another Big Explosion_, and a new LP they plan to record later this summer, LA’s Jr. Juggernaut decided to release this new standalone single just in time for Independence Day. This is the way to start the summer! ![Image 76](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/graham%20parker%202.jpg) ## GRAHAM PARKER & THE GOLDENTOPS – Quality Footwear: Live at the Brook (Big Stir Records, bigstirrecords.bandcamp.com) Graham Parker is an institution. He’s been making music for decades, going back to the 1970's. He’s best known for Graham Parker and the Rumour, but he’s fronted a number of bands over the years, including his most recent, The Goldentops. He writes and performs music that spans genres, including pub rock, power pop, new wave, soul and R&B, sometimes blurring the lines between genres. In 2023, during a UK tour, Parker and The Goldentops had their performance at The Brook in Southampton professionally recorded with the idea of doing some editing, but a live LP is best when the songs speak for themselves, removing most of the stage banter, guitar tuning, and rambling. Big Stir came up with the idea of a limited vinyl release, and this record was born. The LP’s title, “Quality Footwear,” comes from the final two tracks, “Boogie Shoes” and “Soul Shoes.” The former is a KC and the Sunshine Band cover that’s long been a staple of Parker’s sets, while the latter is one of his OG songs from The Rumour days. And on this live date, Rumour guitarist Brinsley Schwarz sat in. If you’ve followed Graham Parker’s career you know exactly what to expect from this album. It’s classic material with plenty of soul and plenty of rockin’. It starts with the folk rock “Hotel Chambermaid,” from his 1976 LP with The Rumour, _Heat Treatment_. “Black Lincoln Continental” is a blues rock tune from 1985 Steady Nerves release by Graham Parker and the Shot. We get some solid soulful post-punk in “Get Started. Start a Fire” off his solo LP, _Mona Lisa’s Sister_, released in 1988. And we get a jazzy country balled, “It Mattered to Me,” from his 2023 Goldentops’ LP, _Last Chance to Learn the Twist_. There are several cuts from that LP here, but the 40+ minute set covers all the Parker eras, focusing most heavily on his earliest and most recent songs. And he can still bring it. Not bad for a 75 year old. ![Image 77](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/quintana.jpg) ## QUINTANA DEAD BLUES EXPERIENCE – Ashes (Adrenalin Fix Music, www.adrenalinfixmusic.com) Bordeaux is most closely associated with fine wine. Formed in 2017 as a solo project by Piero Quintana, the band has evolved into the current powerhouse featuring Quintana and various guests in recordings and live shows. The first few tracks are like this, sludge-filled, metallic hard rock with strong grunge influence, with “What Is Mine” being one of the better tracks. It’s the most grunge-filled with a quicker pace, packed with energy. But then, “Still Haunted” lightens the mood a little bit with something more melodic and solidly in the alt-rock camp. Most of the tracks strike a nice balance, sort of like Queens of the Stone Age or, more aptly, Mudhoney, and some, like “Kinda Low,” feature extended stoner rock jams. ![Image 78](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/spacemoth.jpg) ## SPACEMOTH – Inward Eye (Greenway Records, ssspacemoth.bandcamp.com) Maryam Qudus has been, as she says, “making weird loops with a guitar and a pedal” since she was a teenager. I like “Paper Cup,” for its use of grungy dissonance underneath a lithe indie pop melody, creating a gorgeous contrast. “Cloud of Echoes” is aptly named, because it’s just a wide open sky of beats and ambience flowing and pulsing. And there’s throbbing bass a la Silver Apples in the darkly lush “A Photograph Replaced My Mind,” a song with deep psychedelic roots. Spacemoth may be the work of someone “making weird loops with a guitar and a pedal,” but it’s highly entertaining and enlightening. ![Image 79](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/taxigirls.jpg) ## TAXI GIRLS – Static (Stomp Records, taxigirls.bandcamp.com) Tax

One of the most fun and unique Rev tunes is “3rd & Pike,” an upbeat mix of glam and Zydeco music, complete with accordion, but with dark lyrics about broken trust. Another good one is the hard-driving “Vengeance,” which mixes glam, hard rock, and street punk. Andy Wylie’s songs tend to be smoother, more focused on power pop and melodic punk sounds. “Have a Heart” has a cool bounce, with a dark melodic punk vibe. “Hellish Tattoo” and “Strangled Voices,” too, have a solid 90's melodic punk sound, with parts that are dark and parts that are bright and poppy. Andy’s vocals sometimes verge on crooning, too, reminding me a little bit of Josh Caterer’s vocals with The Smoking Popes. Speaking of which, my favorite Andy song of the album has to be “Burn the Page,” which oozes poppy music and crooning vocals, bouncy and bright, but with lyrics about the terrible state of the world today. “Death of the Optimist” sees a bit of Rev’s street punk vibe seeping into Andy’s pop punk tune, particularly in the chorus. Although it’s pretty easy to tell the difference between songs written by Rev or Andy, one thing they all have in common is their unrelenting energy. Every Drowns song comes across as an unstoppable force. The boys from Seattle have another winner on their hands. ![Image 6](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/goodnightnobody.jpg) ## GOODNIGHT NOBODY (Sweet Cheetah Records, goodnightnobody.bandcamp.com) Debut albums are always fun. Discovering new music from new bands you’ve never heard of before can sometimes be like hitting the lottery. Goodnight Nobody is a trio that hails from Vermont and plays edgy, noisy indie that injects mathish moments, emo influence, and a bit of punch into their music, and this is their debut LP. I can hear the grit of dissonance, twisted rhythms, and melodic hooks, sometimes sounding like a descendant of Dischord Revolution Summer bands, sometimes sounding more like a 90's post-hardcore band. The opening track falls into the latter category, with grinding guitars and fuzz-filled bass. Vocals are emphatically shouted as the beat pulses hypnotically, as the band jams. “(We’ve Got the) Receipts” is a strong mix of strident post hardcore chords and emo melodic lines and vocals. “Can vs. Should” is another that features both melodic indie/emo, but also a jamming bridge that goes hard toward a psych aesthetic. But it’s the more East Coast emo-sounding tracks that really get me going. “Aurora” has a mid-80's Soulside sort of sound, but maybe gliding along a little more smoothly. “Rosary” reminds me a bit of some of the music Gauge (originator of the Midwest emo sound) was making in the early 90's, making it another favorite. I’m sure the fact that the band had J Robbins (Jawbox, J Robbins Band, Government Issue) produce this helped inform the sound. This is a pretty solid debut. ![Image 7](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/thegoods.jpg) ## THE GOODS – Goodbye Summertime (Dandy Boy Records, dandyboyrecords.bandcamp.com) Following their debut EP in 2023, Oakland’s power poppers The Goods released their debut full-length, _Don’t Spoil the Fun_, last year. Now they’re back with their sophomore LP, and _Goodbye Summertime_ is just in time for the changing of the seasons. And one thing I notice about this LP, in comparison to their debut, is that the new songs are smoother and less raucous, with injections of folk-pop and psych. They’ve also got lusher arrangements, with a fuller sound, going beyond the simplicity of guitar-driven rock 'n' roll. The songs are still jangly power pop, just with less of an edge. They feel more like 60's and 70's guitar pop than 80's power pop, with hints of British Invasion era sounds, too. I really like the mod feel of the opening track, “Lazy,” and the delicate nature of “Love You More” is lovely. We get folksy tunes, with acoustic guitar in the mix, like the melancholy “Don’t Worry,” and there’s the jangly upbeat “Summer’s Almost Gone,” a song about making the most of the time we have. The Goods’ new LP is a pleasant one, but I wish it had more of the raucous nature of the EP. ![Image 8](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/madtab.jpg) ## MAD TAB – Alas! The Bomb Voyage… (Innanuttshell Reekordingz, innanuttshellreekordingz.com) Without the press materials telling me that Mad Tab is a Southern California band, I knew it just from listening to the record. Their brand of punk rock contains an aggressive mix of speedy hardcore, beachy pop punk, skanking ska punk, and even some dub reggae influenced music. There’s solid musicianship and an urgent feel to these songs, which sound super-tight without sounding slick, and that’s a perfect combination for me. Almost from the start we get high energy tracks like “Animals,” which has a fantastic rapid-fire rhythm, crunchy hardcore instrumentals, and a great pop melody. It’s one of the standout tracks of an album full of great songs. I love the harmonies in “Awake,” another speedy poppy hardcore tune. We get a slower grind alternating with gritty hardcore in the quintessentially SoCal “Vans On My Feet.” And I love “All Live,” a song that’s blisteringly fast and melodic, poppy and fun. There are a number of solid ska punk tunes here, including “Loose Teeth” and “Good Boi,” both of which have a nice rock steady lope. We get a history lesson, of a sort, in “Windrush Empire,” a song about the effort to rebuild London after World War II and the importation of cheap labor from the Caribbean, which led to Two Tone culture in the UK. “The Process” mixes ska punk with a grittier vibe, with parts of the song sounding like it comes from the backyards of East L.A. “Work N Pressure,” on the other hand, is brisker and more reminiscent of Operation Ivy, with a mix of street punk grit and skankin’ beats. And songs like “Don’t Blink” mix aggressive hardcore with smoother ska sounds to make something that theoretically shouldn’t exist, but is an amazing track worthy of Bad Brains. The album closer is a fun acoustic ska punk track, showing the band’s versatility. Mad Tab is a great band and Alas! The Bomb Voyage… is a great listen. ![Image 9](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/smugbrothers5.jpg) ## SMUG BROTHERS – Pinhole to Vortex (Anyway Records, smugbrothers.bandcamp.com) Dayton, Ohio’s indie-power-pop masters are getting to be quite prolific! It was just this past May yhey released their career retrospective LP, _Gravity Is Just a Way to Fall_. And that came on the heels of a pair of LPs in 2025! On this latest album, they’ve evolved a little bit away from their British Invasion influences and more toward a solid indie-rock sound, but still informed by classic power pop, with a relaxed vibe and a polished sound. Guitars jangle confidently and the tempos are easygoing. Multi-part vocal harmonies abound, and the music is pleasant. I like the lush sounds of “Kind Enough to Share,” and the deep driving sound of “Bolt Through the Blackout” is pretty cool. Smug Brothers’ vibe on this album is reminding me of current Guided By Voices sort of stuff. Which makes sense, because they’re both Ohio bands. I like the retro folk-psych aesthetic of “Wake Up (Be Your Own Planet)” and “Speeding By the Way Things Used to Look,” and the little trumpet fanfare flourishes of “Picasso Waltzes” are nice. If I have one bit of constructive criticism for Smug Brothers, it would be that there’s less variety in the sounds on this album than in the past. A little change now and then, plus more dynamic range can make for a more engaging listening experience. ![Image 10](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/topdown.jpg) ## TOPDOWN – The Earth & All Its Pavement (Sweet Cheetah Records/ Diverse Chorus Records /topdowntx.bandcamp.com) Austin band Topdown may have only been around since 2024 but they’ve hit the ground running and are already releasing their sophomore LP. The five-piece band plays a sweet blend of post-hardcore, emo, and melodic hardcore, their songs filled with crunch, broad, smooth melodies, and a contrasting mix of lush romantic and hard-edged gritty vocals. I love the way the album opens, with “Adrenaline.” We get a background whine and a big clanging bass in the foreground for a few bars, and then the whole band comes in with explosive energy, Grace’s lead vocals croon with passion. The contrast of the hard-edged pummeling instrumentals and the gorgeous torch song vocals is something to behold. “Dissonance,” which follows, is a broad striding track with moments of pure romance, and it’s about not knowing how to love properly, according to Grace. Another favorite is “Coping Mechanism,” which sometimes jangles with dreamy indie pop vibes, and other times hits you square in the jaw with a big one-two combination punch. There’s also the lovely “Interlude,” which is the stuff of sweet dreams, coming right before the album closer, “Sentimental,” a song that leans heavily into the smooth 2000's emo sound. Topdown’s big dynamic range and the ease in which they cross-blend genres makes _The Earth & All Its Pavement_ a winner. ![Image 11](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/yammerjaw.jpg) ## YAMMER JAW – Burth (yammerjaw.bandcamp.com) Hailing from the unlikeliest of places, Nashville, Yammer Jaw is about the furthest from country music you can get. The band’s debut mini-LP is filled with post-hardcore rage, angular melodic lines, shifting rhythms, and manic noise. The band calls it an EP, but with nine tracks and 26 minutes, it’s almost a full album. The PR materials reference Fugazi and Drive Like Jehu as “For Fans Of” bands. I disagree. Yammer Jaw has more of a Quicksand or Refused intensity, with metallic power and frenzy mixed with the manic anxiety of New York’s Alice Donut. Strong points include the expertly rumbling bass, the unpredictable nature of the songs, and the frenetic intensity of it all. It’s an unending sonic assault that will have you jumping and shouting, and your neighbors banging on the walls. Peak Yammer Jaw can be found in “Apex Creditor,” a track that has a great pun for a title, tons of menace, and lots of shifting vibes. “Gun” has some cool gliding moments amidst the chaos, while “Lamp of Freedom” is the most experimental track, less of a song and more meandering noise plus damning sermon. There’s a lot of political commentary in this album, too, such as in the track, “Sheep,” which likens the population to the titular animal, people spending all their time doomscrolling and following the herd. “It’s seven o’clock, do you know where your freedom is?” the track asks. I think we could have done without “Beefy Streams,” though, which is nothing more than 30 seconds of men peeing into a toilet. But other than that, this is a big muscular debut. * * * ![Image 12](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/bethcameron.jpg) ## BETH CAMERON – The World. Oh No. (Submissive Grin, bethcameronmusic.bandcamp.com) Beth Cameron is, apparently, a big deal in the local Nashville indie music scene. It’s a scene that’s, sadly, overshadowed by the country music industry and doesn’t get the recognition it deserves. I can vouch for that, because I was unfamiliar with Cameron, though this has, thankfully, been corrected. She’s played in various bands, including Forget Cassettes and Black Bra, but The World, Oh No. is her solo debut. The best way I can describe the music on this album is experimental pop music. The songs are mysterious and morose, and they range from subdued to grand. These songs are more aptly described as sonic artwork, with varied textures and tones. There is much darkness and sadness, the instrumentals filled with an undercurrent of noise and whispers, and Cameron’s vocals are pure beauty. After the short introductory “Prodrome,” which introduces an eerie theme that recurs at the end of the album, “Something in the Offing” feels tentative and apprehensive. Piano and drums provide a dirge-like atmosphere, as Cameron’s angelic voice trembles with unease. “Lemonsqueezer,” which follows, reminds me of Laurie Anderson’s performance art music, alternating between spoken word and smooth singing, but the lyrics are dark and devastating. The celestial singing at the end is in stark contrast to the lyrics about a woman who has suffered horribly from abuse, lived with suicidal ideations, and self-medicated to dull the pain. Another standout is “Sympathetic Symphony,” a song with the sound of dystopian science fiction. It’s noisy and dark, with an emphatic rhythm. Halfway through the track, the question comes, “Are you okay?” and the floodgates are opened with loud uncontrolled sobbing. The album’s lead single “HeLa” is huge and bold spacy progressive art rock, reminiscent of Pink Floyd. It tells the true story of a woman, HeLa (Henrietta Lacks), who died of cervical cancer at age 31 in 1951. Doctors harvested her cancer cells, without her knowledge or consent, and that became the first immortalized cell line in medical science. Her cells have been used in countless studies, fueling vaccines for polio, HPV, and COVID-19, and contributing to HIV/AIDs and cancer research. Her family members didn’t even know about this until the 1970s, and there have been legal settlements over this. She may have died, but she has saved millions of lives. She is eternal and everlasting. I love “RIP, OP,” which begins as a simple lament, complete with electric organ and backing vocal choir, giving it a very spiritual feel. But halfway through the organ is replaced by a piano, and the song takes on the vibe of an off-Broadway stage production. And the closing title track, subtitled “Postdrome,” has a truly post-apocalyptic vibe. The wind howls, an out of tune piano pecks out that introductory melody we heard at the beginning of the record, and then we hear a chorus of voices whispering and crying, “Oh no!” This reaches a frenzy and is suddenly cut, replaced with a high pitched tone, background hiss, and solemn voice intoning, “I thought that you were an anchor in the drift of the world. But, no, there isn’t an anchor anywhere. There isn’t an anchor in the drift of the world. Oh, no. I thought you were. Oh, no. The drift of the world.” It’s the stuff of nightmares. Throughout the nearly hour-long album, we’re taken on a journey and confronted. There are uncomfortable truths here that most would not care to admit. It’s difficult, and compelling. It’s outstanding art.![Image 13](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/gay%20agenda.jpeg) ## THE GAY AGENDA – Pink Noise (thegayagenda.bandcamp.com) We’ve heard it repeatedly from Christian Conservatives: “They’re trying to push the gay agenda into our lives!” But "they" don’t know what the real gay agenda is, and this San Diego queer hardcore band is here to give you a crash course. This is the band’s third release, and their second LP, after 2018’s self-titled double flexi-disc EP and 2020’s one-sided LP (it was on clear vinyl, with the B-side being a silk-screen of the band’s logo). Their short homocore blasts have typically been chaotic and noisy, like a lot of modern hardcore, but this new LP features more melody and better production quality, so you can really hear the songs. They’re still powerful and edgy, with speedy pounding songs, huge power chords, thumping bass lines, and angry vocals. You still best not try anything homophobic with them around, if you know what’s good for you. Because the gay agenda ain’t all about same sex love. For example, “Eye for an Eye” is about the new consequences for gay bashing. No, you won’t get away with it anymore, because it’s eye for an eye time, and they don’t intend to let you walk away. The gay agenda also includes encouraging people to be their authentic selves. “Sissy Boy,” which opens the LP, speaks to how queer boys have been told to act straight to be safe in the world, but how this causes conflict of self: “All the years spent hiding / I can no longer tell / Which face is truly my own / Or the lie I’ve used as a shield.” The music is angular and cuts like a knife, pounding unrelentingly. There’s a song about standing up for yourself (“Find Your Voice”), and a song about government silence during the AIDS crisis (“Vale of Tears”). There’s a refresher for young queers who weren’t alive before the Supreme Court struck down anti-sodomy laws or when states began legalizing same-sex marriage; “Hid the Truth” is about how in the post-World War II era of supposed growing freedom and prosperity for all Americans, gay people were still persecuted and prosecuted – it was illegal to be gay in many places. The title track is about the apolitical gays, who “want glitter with no political voice,” who just want to know “Who’s your favorite drag queen? What’s your drug of choice?” They reject militant political messages, because they’re no better than the Christian Nationalists in that they are only interested in associating with people like themselves, and they perpetrate the “straight-washing” of views that don’t match their own. Probably the most important song of the album is “Sigh of Relief.” It speaks to how all oppressed people need to stand together and fight for each other’s rights. Just because gay and lesbian people have earned some level of equal rights (for now) doesn’t mean sighing in relief and thinking the fight is over. You can’t say “It’s not my fight / When black lives killed by police.” You can’t say “It’s them not me / Don’t want to hear a speech / When Trans lives are killed in gay streets.” The song reminds us of the allies that fought for gay rights, and now we all need to work together to secure equal rights for everyone. Don’t say it’s not your fight because your skin is white or because you’re cis-gendered. And as the song that follows (“Architects”) says, we have to “Stop drawing lines in our community / Don’t argue with me about your selfish identity / Together we fight as a voice against impunity / Then why only Pride, do you claim our unity? / Disdainful of our sisters, we’re the architects of our own demise.” In other words, united we stand, divided we fall, as the old saying goes. With better sound quality, less chaos and more discernable melodic lines, and growled vocals in which you can actually hear the important words of the lyrics, Pink Noise is The Gay Agenda’s best release yet.![Image 14](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/surulin.jpg) ## SURALIN – Every Day Slices Me (itselevenrecords.bandcamp.com) After 17 years as a band and having released five LPs, Chemnitz, Germany-based Suralin are releasing their very first 7” EP! Chemnitz is located in the German state of Saxony, deep in the heart of the former German Democratic Republic (East Germany). It’s unlikely the members of the band have any memory of the period when their country was a Soviet satellite; they may well have not even been alive when Germany reunited in 1990. Their music, therefore, has none of the austerity one associates with Soviet era music. Indeed, there’s more resemblance to the Krautrock of the 1960s and 1970s with pounding minimalist rhythms. But they blend these rhythms with lush dreamy indie pop and create mesmerizing music. There’s an urgency to the four songs on the EP, which comes from that insistent rhythm. The guitars jangle vehemently, the bass thrumming away to the beat, but the vocals are smooth and beautiful. The A-side features two songs in this vein, “Driving Home” and the title track, and though the B-side songs are cohesive, they change things up somewhat. “The Sentiment’s a Lie” is a little slower and smoother, with a jazzy vibe. And “I Love a Boy” is harder and noisier, with a bigger, more open sound. This is a compelling EP that I highly recommend. * * * ![Image 15](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/antietam.jpg) ## ANTIETAM – The Counting Game (Dromedary Records, dromedaryrecords.bandcamp.com) Antietam is a storied name in the world of underground rock music. Founded more than four decades ago by guitarist/vocalist Tara Key and bassist Tim Harris, the band has evolved over time, through an early art punk and experimental spimd to raucous, punk-inspired indie. As with most of us, they’ve slowed things down over the years, and nowadays focus on ambient and folk-inspired tunes. And, to be very honest, I prefer their earlier music, because it was higher energy and had more vitality and adventure in it. _The Counting Game_, to my ears, is just too relaxed, feeling almost lackadaisical. The songs are smooth and flowy, but there’s not a lot of energy behind them. The textures are nice, with a dreamy post-punk sort of sound, but there’s also a lot of country twang, including banjo, and songs that drone repetitively. Even when they get grittier, like on “The Finest Line,” the pace drags, Tara Key shows she’s still a guitar master, and I do like some of the cool jazz tone of “Every Other Star,” but it just doesn’t feel like they’re excited to be playing these songs. Even on “Coco Bella,” which also uses jazz beats, trumpet, and piano, it just doesn’t have that verve I expected. This disappointed me. ![Image 16](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/Armsandarmor.jpg) ## ARMS & ARMOUR – The Hunted (Sweet Cheetah Records / Steadfast Records, steadfastrecords.com) Arms & Armour are the dystopian soundtrack of the modern world. The duo of Lauren Voss (vocals, guitar, and synths) and John Panza (drums, drum machine programming, guitar, and synths) play music that’s a mix of industrial, goth, doom, and icy cold post punk. Guitars are heavy and sludgy, the vocals melancholic, and the tempos are slow and deliberate. The result is the music that foretells of existential threat in a post-apocalyptic world. We hear the wind howling in the empty places, and echoes of the past that we all ignored that, had we listened, could have prevented the fate in which we find ourselves. Angular laments are juxtaposed against drum and bass beats, while guitar dissonance expresses how broken the world is. This is the slower drugged out vision that Future Sounds of London gave us on their _Dead Cities_ album. There’s something hypnotic and brooding in the music, something that gives succor in the bleakness of life. Hang in there. All is not lost. The album ends with a delicate sign of hope with “Ash’s Song.” Maybe this isn’t the end. Somber and reflective. ![Image 17](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/cuvabimo.jpg) ## CUVA BIMÖ – New Western Values (Sell the Heart Records, cuvabimo.bandcamp.com) They proudly call themselves a “post-whatever rock” band, and that is fairly apt for the Bay area quartet made up of Sebastian Moeller (guitar, vocals), Pete Vadelnieks (guitar, vocals), Jake Bilich (bass), and Ricky Cunliffe (drums). The band formed in response to a Craigslist ad, and considered calling themselves "Craigslist Hook Up,” but decide against it (for now). The band’s style is a mélange of post punk, indie, garage, noise rock, grunge, and art punk, exhibiting elements of all of these but falling solely into none of those camps. After the decidedly experimental instrumental, “4 A.M. Somewhere,” which opens the album, we get the quirky title track, which features grunge-filled guitars and bass, an angular melodic line, and eccentric vocal delivery. The track is chaotic and offbeat, with many unexpected twists and turns. It makes it my kind of track! And that’s the sort of thing we get throughout the ten tracks, gritty noisy instrumentals and vocals that are very much in the art punk vein. It’s like their genre is one of structured disorder. There’s chaos and mayhem, yet it’s controlled and managed to produce these songs. I like the powerful vocals and post punk melodic line of “Charm Offensive,” while “800 Meter Tears” mixes the art punk aesthetic with mathy goth guitars and funky bass. The minimalist melody of “Sound and Fury” is hypnotic, and the deep gravelly vocals are a stark contrast to the gliding instrumentals. Sounding very different, “Malagradecido” is sung in Spanish and has deep garage rock roots. And the closing track, “Too Much,” is not enough! It’s psych! It’s grunge! It’s art punk! It’s all of these and none of them! It’s the genius of CuVa Bimö! ![Image 18](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/wesleystace.jpg) ## WESLEY STACE – One Last Heist (Pravda Records, wesleystace.bandcamp.com) Previously recording under the name John Wesley Harding, Wesley Stace has reverted to his birth name more recently for his music. He’s also a well-known author of four novels, including the international best-seller _Misfortune_. He’s also recorded duets with Bruce Springsteen, Lou Reed, and Rosanne Cash, among others, and has created Cabinet of Wonders, a cabaret-style show that plays regularly in New York City and features a rotating cast of performers. He has taught at Princeton, Swarthmore, and Farleigh-Dickinson and writes for the Times Literary Supplement and the Wall Street Journal. It’s safe to say Stace is a modern day renaissance man. His UK origins (he was born in East Sussex) are on display in his music, which has a bit of 1980's Stiff Records vibe to it, and there’s also a little Billy Joel, a bit of Elvis Costello, and loads of old school jazzy pop music. A lot of the songs are quite clever or tell interesting stories, like the title track, which opens the album. The titular activity is what happens when a master thief is pulled in from retirement for one last job, and it immediately reminds me of the Stiff Records era, with a jazzier, smoother Ian Dury sound. It’s about taking that one last risk that, if it works out, will set you for your golden years, but if it doesn’t there could be dire consequences. Songs like “Penelope” are what give me the Elvis Costello impression, an ode to a woman with the same kind of lovely pop ballad, just a bit jazzed up. I enjoy the finger-snapping “Get It in Your Fingers,” a quietly hopping tune that features a circle of fifths chord progression at one point. “I Say Lots of Things” is a smooth song about a smooth talker who lies easily and takes advantage of the good nature of others. And “Thoughts and Prayers” is simply a wonderful piano ballad, about how people put blinders on and don’t care to do anything about the misfortunes of others until it happens to them. It’s about how politicians do nothing but offer “thoughts and prayers,” leaving people to continue suffering. A lovely album. ![Image 19](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/STETSONHEATSEEKER.jpg) ## STETSON HEAT SEEKER – This Is No Place for Cowards (stetsonheatseeker.bandcamp.com) Stetson Heat Seeker is a newer band, formed in 2023 in Seattle, Washington. They quickly released a mini-LP and began playing shows around town, and then went though a series of personnel changes leading us to the current lineup of Ian Read (lead vocals, guitar), Megan Slavich (bass, backing vocals), Joshua Ihler (drums, percussion, backing vocals), Katie Cassidy (tenor sax, lead and backing vocals), and Madison Moilanen (guitar, tambourine, backing vocals). Given the band name and the sound, you might be forgiven for thinking they’re from Texas, because they’ve got a distinctly cow-punk vibe, but it’s heavy frenetic stuff, mixing in a bit of surf punk, and the tenor sax gives the songs are powerfully gritty and soulful sound. The lead vocals are manic and strong, and the overall sound reminds me of China’s Round Eye, but maybe with a funkier edge. The overall tone is sharp and biting, with loads of fuzz in the bass, and the energy level is off the charts. Heat seeking indeed! These cowboys are the kind that’ll come home covered in dust and dirt and aren’t afraid to mix it up and get into some trouble. “Cultbreaker” is a perfect opener, strong and dark controlled chaos. There’s a great loping ode to working hard while remaining in poverty with “Minimum Wage.” There’s more not-giving-a-fuck than anger, and plenty of sarcasm. I really like the surfy garage punk vibes of “Sharpshooter,” a song about the stupid risks people take, often in pursuit of sex or love, using a sharpshooter show as a metaphor. The pursuit of feeling good (if you know what I mean) is the topic of the super sleazy “Oh Sweet Pain,” with a repeating riff and lyrics that’ll have you jonesing for what it is you want. And “Trouble Finds You,” the penultimate track, is a solid standout, with a dark, evil, twisted circus sound. If you get cold, don’t worry about seeking heat, seek this record instead. ![Image 20](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/stillinsane.jpg) ## STILL INSANE – When Friendship Is Not Enough (Thousand Islands Records, thousandislandsrecords.ca) This record is a perfect example of why putting one of the best tracks first is so important. When I first started listening to the first track, “Intro,” and even the title track that follows, my reaction was that this band sounds like that local hardcore band from the outer edges of the metro area that’s populated by older dudes who never outgrew the 1980's. You know the ones, the guys who still wear mohawks in their 50's and 60's and who only listen to early 80's hardcore on repeat. They’re awful, but they open for every touring hardcore band that comes through town. We all have ‘em. I almost gave up on the record, but that’s not me, I give everything a fair chance. Good thing I did, because the quality improved dramatically. That intro made me think this was going to be some metallic prog-rock band, while the title track is generic thrashy speed-core with out-of-tune gang vocals singing the chorus, which consists of just the name of the song. The lead vocals are spoken-shouted in a fairly generic “hardcore” way. It’s honestly a mess. As the album progresses, though, the songs improve. There’s loping poppy crunchy punk rock in “Do What You Want” and “Missed It Again,” which are couple of the best tracks of the album, but most of it features dark, speedy, 90's skate-punk. The instrumentals are well done, but the one thing that bothered me is that the vocals are a little problematic, with some pitch issues. ![Image 21](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/strangebirds.jpg) ## STRANGE BIRDS – Little Victories (Sweet Cheetah Records, strangebirdssongs.bandcamp.com) Back in the 90's, I remember Louisville as having some good bands that featured an emo or post hardcore sound. Bands like Metroschifter, Shipping News, Sunspring, Slint, and more were putting out great records. Strange Birds adds to this legacy, though featuring a transplant from Kansas City, Missouri. Brandon Butler, the guitarist and vocalist, is better known from his time in Boys Life, while drummer Ella Jean Jumpkins and bassist Brian Meurer are homegrown talents, having grown up playing in bands in the local Louisville scene (note, this recording features Matt Olsen on bass). The songs on this LP have a subdued, pensive quality, as one might expect given their homebase and pedigree. But even within this they’ve got a wide range of sounds going on. The album opens with jangly indie pop in the title track, and immediately after we get the understated indie blended with a bit of Americana of “BMX Summer” and “Take You Anywhere.” “The Old House” starts out with a striding indie sound, but as the song evolves, the guitar takes on a bit of 80s goth tone for a time. I really like “Darker Still,” which is one of the more wistful songs, starting tentatively, but getting thicker and more emphatic as the song grows. The use of a guitar wailing in the background is very effective at setting a tone, as are the whispery vocals. As the song fades out, there are ghostly whispers and ambient sounds, providing an air of mystery. “Roll with the Punches” feels out of place after that. It’s another pleasant slow head-bobber that mixes hazy indie with an Americana twang that fits in better with the earlier part of the album. But it’s with the penultimate track, “Blood Currents,” that the album hits its heights, in my opinion. It’s the most experimental track of the album, featuring a meandering melody and a spoken word track buried in the mix that consists of deep buzzing bass, softly tentative drums, and lush guitars. It’s a gorgeous sonic piece of art. The album closes with “Deleted Scenes,” which brings in a noisy indie sound and a song about the dismantling of the “American Dream,” and how it’s become nothing but a series of “deleted scenes,” everything good about life being cut away from us. I miss listening to the music coming out of Louisville. But now we have Strange Birds, and they’re a worthy heir to the mantle.![Image 22](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/thermals2.jpg) ## THE THERMALS – Under Crushing Rain (Static Catsup Aspic, thethermals.bandcamp.com) OMG, they’re back! The Portland band that was formed way back in 2002, survived multiple lineup changes and formally disbanded in 2018 has returned, now as a solo project of founder Hutch Harris. The band was much beloved in their heyday, releasing seven studio LPs and a bunch of EPs and singles. They played a mix of pop punk-influenced indie rock and indie pop. I remember seeing them play live on multiple occasions, and thinking they were a pleasant enough band, but too many of their songs sounded alike to my ears to be a real stand-out band. Now, ten years after the release of their last album, _We Disappear_, and after the December 2025 announcement of Harris’ return as The Thermals, a new album, _Under the Crushing Rain,_ brings the return of The Thermals. And while the music is not quite as lo-fi as the band was known for, the poppy punk-informed indie rock is still there. Harris’ unique vocal stylings are still there. But what’s great about this album is that, even though the sound is still distinctly The Thermals, there’s more variety in the ten songs offered here than I ever remember hearing when they were a touring band. The music still features emphatic rhythms, but the tone varies from the darkness of “Good Morning Fellow Scavengers” to the incongruently bright “Dark, Dark Place,” the latter being a bouncy song about wanting to both eschew the past, but not to erase it, to sit with it, experience it, but not get stuck in it. There are songs that, while slower, have a stronger bounce and a soulful feel, like “Spirit Collectors,” and there are songs that are breezy folky pop, like “In the Flow.” I love the clean guitar tone on this one, especially in the short guitar solo, and Harris’ vocals give it a nerd-pop vibe that’s appealing. There’s 50’s early rock and roll thing going on with “I Will Be Delivered,” and the title track that closes the LP is an impossibly happy sounding song with very dark lyrics. The variety, the arrangements that feature strong keyboards, and the solid songwriting mean that not only are The Thermals back, it means Harris has released the best Thermals album yet. Now he needs to recruit some people to take this show on the road! ![Image 23](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/firesalecorpsplit.jpg) ## FIRE SALE / THE CORPS – Split Decision split EP (Negative Progression Records, www.negativeprogressionrecords.com) Two bands, two sides, two songs each are what we get on this new split EP featuring Fire Sale and The Corps. Fire Sale features seasoned veterans from familiar bands: Pedro Aida from Ann Beretta, ShotClock, and The Iron Roses takes up vocal duties; Chris Swinney of The Ataris, Brazil, and Underminded is the lead guitarist; Matt Riddle (Face to Face, No Use for a Name, Pulley) is the bassist; Brad Edwards (Weaver Street) plays rhythm guitar; and Matt Morris (Darlington, Down By Law) is on drums. Their tracks sound just like you might imagine coming from a supergroup lineup like this: powerful, melodic, and crunchy. Their first track, “Kill the Noise,” is a dark loping track that speaks about mental health, while the politically charged “Dies Irae” is a little poppier, a little faster, and more frantic, in a Descendents sort of vein. Flipping the record over reveals two tracks from Vancouver’s The Corps. They may be lesser known, but they’ve been around for over a decade, and they offer up a couple of speedy skate-punk tracks in a 90's vein. The music is fast and crisp, yet always melodic. Their first song, “Imposter Syndrome,” is an ode to something we all feel from time to time, some more than others. In the case of The Corps, it’s about sharing the stage with their musical heroes (they’ve toured with Ignite and Strung Out, for example) and feeling unworthy. The second track is a little smoother and introspective, and arguably better. “Another World” is one of the band’s comic-book inspired songs (apparently many of their songs are inspired by comics, particularly the DC Universe). Solid split. * * * ![Image 24](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/ballyhoo.jpg) ## BALLYHOO! – Bad Summer (Right Coast Records, www.rightcoastrecords.com) Maryland band Ballyhoo! have been making music for the past three decades. They’ve been described as a “reggae rock” band, but this album is almost entirely slick 1990s/2000s pop punk in the vein of stalwarts of the era like Blink 182 or Sum 41. Which makes sense when you note that this new album was produced by John Feldmann, who’s produced Blink, as well as Good Charlotte, Panic! At the Disco, Avril Lavigne, and Goldfinger (his own band). It’s the slick generic pop punk sound that filled the airwaves in the 90s and early 2000s, and, as such, does nothing for me. And I guess there’s some mild reggae-pop on the record, but it’s super watered down and whitewashed. “Cali Girl” and “Long Weekend” fall into this category, but it’s about the only music even close to reggae on the album. “Happy” features a couple of alto saxophone solos that makes the song sound like something from the SNL band. And “I Guess I’ll Go Fuck Myself” is really unfortunate song that wishes harm on others, with lyrics that include “I still wish you would die.” I guess it’s about people who troll on the internet, and cause emotional distress to others, but still… If you’re a Blink fan, you may like this record, but I’m not a fan. ![Image 25](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/generacion.jpg) ## GENERACIÓN SUICIDA – Hombre Nuevo (Vitriol Records, www.vitriolrecords.com) Generación Suicida, hailing from Los Angeles, presents a dark, dusty lonely sort of post punk vision. The band shows their garage punk roots on some songs, with some rapid downstroke strumming, but most of the songs have a slower, more introspective feel, filled with atmosphere. The songs are all sung in Spanish, so it’s hard to for me to know what they’re singing about. But most of the songs sure are morose. Some, though, have a more urgent feel, like “Desilucion,” sung with gritty vocals to give it an edge. The title translates to “Disillusion” or “Disappointment,” so take your cue from that as to what the song is about. It’s not a happy thing. “Oscuridad” is one of those garage punk tunes, with a livelier feel and a quicker pace. But the gorgeous reverb-laden guitar gives it that mournful sound, appropriate for a song whose title means “Darkness.” “Golpe Al Barrio” (Blow to the Neighborhood), too, has a bit more bounce to it, but it also has a menacing tone. Things are not looking up in the barrio, that’s for sure. One of my favorite songs of the album is “Tres.” It’s a simple enough song, but there’s some cool tension effects from the guitars inserted into the music, and a dark surf punk melodic line. And that surf guitar sound returns on “A Los ue Deje Atras” (To Those I Left Behind), which closes the album. The ten songs fully convey a sense of despair – it’s not necessary to understand Spanish to get the emotional content of these songs. Generación Suicida paint a bleak picture of the present, and offer little hope for the future. Recommended. ![Image 26](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/hovland.jpg) ## HOLSMAN – Sally (theholsman.bandcamp.com) Holsman is the eponymous Chicago band led by Ryan Holsman and Dan Tinkler. _Sally_ is a concept album that explores the pair’s experiences as victims of child abuse and how that impacts their abilities to form relationships in adulthood. For example, the lead single, “I’ll Be a Dog in My Next Life” speaks to how even coming back as a dog is no guarantee of a happy life. We all think of pets as receiving unconditional love, but shitty people are always shitty, even kicking their dog, as described in the song. Even the promise that “I’ll be a good boy” is no guarantee of decent treatment, as the song recounts being left alone for hours and feeling that everything bad that happens is your own fault. The band plays a brand of punk-inspired indie rock, with full-on melodies and lush arrangements, vocals packing an emotional wallop. Think Against Me! or a more engaging version of Menzingers. There’s a rawness to the music, a sharp edge to the songs, and they cut deep. You can sense the explosive temper in “Tantrum,” vocals and music going from calm to intense shouting and violence and back again, while always remaining fully tuneful. I really like the opening track, “God’s Drunkest Driver,” which tells a story about Sally, giving the album its title. It uses a '60's pop rock melody and contrasts it with a gruff grunge arrangement. And “Silent Protagonist” alternates between powerful grunge and smoother indie rock. An outlier, sounding very different from the other tracks, is “Perfect! Thank You!” It’s a smoother breezier sound, with lyrics about how, in our adult lives, we do all sorts of things to put on a façade, a false image to the rest of the world, hiding our pains and anxieties from others, using chemicals to maintain the ruse. Listening to these songs makes me want to give Holsman a hug and tell him everything will be OK. This is a solidly good debut LP. ![Image 27](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/jayhawks.jpg) ## THE JAYHAWKS – Sanctuary Park (jayhawksofficial.com) The Jayhawks are a long-standing (on-again, off-again) band that formed over four decades ago in Minneapolis. They’ve had a couple of hiatuses in the intervening years, but here they are, back with another release to add to their massive catalog. They’ve been labeled an “alternative country rock” band in the past, and sure, about half of the songs on _Sanctuary Park_ have a twang, but I hear a lot of influence from power-pop and even indie-rock in this album, showing how they remain a vital and evolving band even after all this time. The arrangements are lush, with multi-part vocal harmonies, acoustic and electric guitars, and keyboards. Country rock songs include “Mr. Lincoln,” which has a Beatles meets honky-tonk vibe, and “Hands Upon the Wheel,” which includes some subtle steel pedal guitar and a dark storytelling sound. “Leap of Faith” is straight-up honky-tonk, with piano, mandolin, and accordion, sounding like something that we might have heard on the old Prairie Home Companion radio show. But other songs are much more power-pop and indie, and more to my tastes. “Keeping Our Heads Above Water” and “Kingston Girl,” the opening pair of tracks on the LP, have a great '80's alternative rock sound, nice and smooth. “American Midnight” is a favorite, for its breezy sound that straddles between alt-country and indie. Then there’s the title track, with a completely different sound than anything else on the album, with a mix of Pink Floyd smooth psych and folk rock storytelling. The Jayhawks are that rare band from way back when that aren’t content to rest on their laurels and just play the old “hits,” and who want to keep making new music. And I’m here for that. ![Image 28](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/startercar.jpg) ## STARTER CAR – Afterlight (startercar.bandcamp.com) Here’s an album from another band that’s been called “country-influenced,” but I don’t see it at all here. What I hear is gorgeously understated indie with hints of folk influence. The pretty arrangements belie the dark subject matter, such as on the opening track, “Throwing Down,” which is about how one might spiral out of control when finding one’s self alone for the weekend. “I’m in trouble when I’m not around you / I drink doubles when I’m not around you,” the song opens. The easy relaxed lope of the song is at odds with the tailspin of bad choices. The songs feature a lovely blend of acoustic and electric instruments, giving the songs a contemplative sound, something appropriate for the self-examination of the songs. I love how “Avert” starts out so quietly, with throbbing guitar lines, and how it grows to a huge emotional swell by the end of the track. I adore the breezy “Wisecrack,” with guitar and violin intertwining and echoing the melody. And right after is the jaunty waltz time “More Me.” This pair of tracks are probably my favorites of the album, and placing them together is brilliant tracking. Overall, I really like the relaxed yet introspective vibe of these songs. Nicely done. ![Image 29](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/johnvanderslice.jpg) ## JOHN VANDERSLICE – Focus (johnvanderslice.bandcamp.com) John Vanderslice has declared he was done writing song lyrics. “I have nothing more to say,” he announced. Recently having relocated from Los Angeles to The Netherlands, his wife Maria convinced him that he should continue singing and writing music, and she would write the lyrics. So the pair teamed up with producer James Riotto and set up about making this album filled with a compelling mix of electric and acoustic, with synths, saxophone, and guitar. Experimental and traditional songcraft collide and meld together. Vanderslice had spent time experimenting with electronic music, and though it’s nice to have his voice back, it was time well-spent. The synths give a nice texture to the songs, from an avant garde edge to lush arrangements. It gives the songs a unique twist and that bit of “extra.” I love the opening track, “From the Life of Marionettes,” which blends acoustic guitars with lush flutes and saxophones and off-kilter electronic interjections. There a cool bossa nova undercurrent to the track, too, particularly in the rhythm and percussion. It’s a wonderful reintroduction, and a gorgeous new sound. The song was inspired by an Ingmar Bergman film John and Maria watched, and warns the listener of the untrustworthiness of the narrator/singer. There are lines that seem both meaningless and profound at the same time, like “I speak in words and colors I cannot see.” There’s a dark dusty vibe in “Steep Land Surveyor,” Vanderslice’s voice sometimes cracking with emotion, the upright bass giving the song a wonderful warmth, adding a hint of jazziness to the arrangement. There are some wonderful instrumentals here, too, including the tentative sounds of “Chopped Piano,” featuring cut up and reassembled bits of piano, synth, and melodic vocalizations. There’s a confessional quality to “Chasing My Blues,” with a melancholy ballad quality and lyrics like “I’ve done drugs my whole life /As much or as little as I like / But this might be the end of the line.” The song seems to be about trying to be better, with the refrain, “Chasing my blues away.” The closing track, “Hold My Head,” is jaw-dropping, with the sound of a post-apocalyptic science-fiction soundtrack. And “jaw-dropping” is a good descriptor for the whole album. It’s that good. ![Image 30](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/vista%20blue%20champtions.jpg) ## VISTA BLUE – Championship of Love (wearevistablue.bandcamp.com) Vista Blue are back, stronger than ever, putting out new songs with furious frequency! And we’re all the better for that. And because Vista Blue’s Mike Patton loves topical tunes, this time out the opening of college football season is the inspiration for songs that use football as a metaphor for relationships. The signature Vista Blue buzzy guitars, keyboards, and Ramones-core vibe are on full display in the pair of tracks that feature a mid-tempo pace and Patton’s casual yet sincere vocals. The “A” side title track is about relationships as competition and trying to figure out a winning strategy, while the “B” side, “She’s My Taysom Hill,” likens romantic love to sports idol worship (Taysom Hill is an NFL player with the New Orleans Saints, and previously played for the Green Bay Packers and the BYU Cougars in college). New Vista Blue songs are always welcome, even when they come fast and furious! ![Image 31](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/winelips.jpg) ## WINE LIPS – TV Dinner (Stomp Records, stomprecords.com) What happens when you mix garage rock, psych, and punk rock? You get Wine Lips, of course! You get 13 hard-driving tracks of manic music, with a frenetic pace and explosive energy. Lo-fi recording and snotty attitude are the order of the day, and the band is like a mainlined injection of adrenaline to remind you that you’re still alive. This is the music your mother warned you about, it’s the seedy club down the alley that smells of urine and weed. It’s all the good times you’ve ever thought about but can’t remember, because of course you can’t remember that night. Though most of the songs are speedy, crunchy, and sassy, “Trip to the Doctor” slows things down; it’s the morning after hangover, until you use the meds the “doctor” gives you to wake you back up, and it starts speeding with more power and energy. One of the most psychedelic tracks of the album is “Leech.” Though it’s still down and dirty garage grit, there’s a definite '60's psych vibe injected into the veins of this beast, and it’s like a warm wave washing over a frozen shoreline. And “Giant Man Baby,” too, is loaded with psych characteristics and gives the impression the we’re listening to the music in the static between two radio stations as we explore the universe by looking through both ends of a telescope at the same time. “Thirst Trap” snaps you back to reality, but you suddenly realize that something’s gone horribly wrong in your absence of mind, and you need to catch up fast! But you’re falling further and further behind, even as you keep running faster and faster. The high cost of living is decried in “Semi Detached Furnished Home,” with complaints about not being able to afford, rent, groceries, or gas. I love the frigid shimmer that yields to the hard rocking nature of “Fried V,” and we’re brought back to that seedy urine and weed soaked alley with “Strip Club DJ,” with its cheesy sleezy glamour: “Twenty bucks is all it takes / It won’t last long but it sure feels great! / If you do it right you can get on stage / Someone check his balls, is he doing OK?” After listening to this record, my balls are more than OK. Highly recommended! * * * ![Image 32](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/deadsealords.jpg) ## DEAD SEA LORDS – "God Can’t Count" EP (Belladonna Records, belladonna-records.com) Noisy and chaotic, yet eminently emotional and powerful, would be one way to describe Gainesville’s Dead Sea Lords. This six-song EP follows their 2024 self-titled debut LP, pretty much picking up where they left off. The music drives hard, but it also throbs hypnotically. I hear elements of early Midwest emo and late period hardcore, giving the songs a definite mid-to-late 80s vibe. But the distortion and anarchic tumult give the songs a vital modern edge. The performances are so raw and energetic, the record sounds more like a live show than a studio recording. ![Image 33](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/getarounds.jpg) ## THE GET AROUNDS – Going Out Tonight (thegetaroundsarenumber1. bandcamp.com) The Get Arounds are one of many bands formed during the COVID pandemic. They began with songwriter and guitarist Carman Lethbridge and drummer Lana Ryma starting to write together, and with Ryma deciding to come out from behind the drumkit and become the lead vocalist. Jay Solyom was recruited to take the drumming spot, with Lethbridge multitasking on guitar, bass, keyboards and backing vocals (the live lineup also features Sean Stubbs, Lisa Lloyd, and Kimi Mah)._Going Out Tonight_ is the band’s sophomore LP, following 2023’s _I Wanna Live_. It features a baker’s dozen tracks that range widely, from hard rock to power pop, glam rock, and even into indie rock territory. The huge variety makes the album feel a little disjointed, with some really solid songs and some that fall miserably flat. One rule I learned a long time ago about tracking albums is always put one of your best songs first. It’s the way you can capture a listener’s attention and the way to get music critics to keep listening. The Get Arounds have not heeded this advice, because “Fuck Around” is a hard rock mess with vocal tuning problems. Nevertheless, I kept listening. The first half of the album is nothing to write home about, sounding more like a high school rock and roll band than a group of professional musicians. Tempos are lazy, and the music feels like stale leftovers from the 70s. “Waiting for the Stars” is no better that the first track. And “Kill or Be Killed” is super cheesy. The arrangements in most of the first half of the album are too thin and there’s just not much energy in the songs. The title track may be the worst offender of the album in this respect. One exception is “Bones,” which is more of an 80s pop rock ballad. It sounds very different from the other tracks in this part of the record, and the vocals are more tuneful, so it’s more successful. But once we get to the second half of the album, things begin to improve. The songs drop the hard rock pretense and focus on more of an indie rock sound, with better sounding vocals and smoother arrangements. “Black Corvette” takes things up a notch from the preceding tracks, and “Hideaway” is a real standout with a poppy punky indie rock vibe and just a bit of 80s influence. “Do Or Die” mixes dark power pop with indie rock, and is another pleaser. Unfortunately, the last few tracks of the album return to more of the cheesy hard rock sound. I just couldn’t get into this. ![Image 34](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/mental%20gymnast.jpg) ## MENTAL GYMNAST – "EP2" (Say-10 Records, www.say-10.com) Mental Gymnast is really hitting the ground running. After releasing their debut EP this past winter, they’re back with five more songs of crunchy old-school hardcore meets synth-punk. Dark melodies, angry vocals, and big gang vocals mix with manic synths to create something that reminds me of Artless, the 80s hardcore band fronted by Maximum Rock’n’Roll’s Mykel Board. And once again they pack a lot into a short amount of time; the five songs occupy a mere six and a half minutes. We get the obsessive “Romance Novels,” with the verses narrated like a twisted story and the chorus gang shouted, the synths swirling around madly and the guitars, bass, and drums providing a solid crunch. I like the hollow sound of “I Want to Believe,” and the crazed speed and screaming of “The Lowest Bar.” Mental Gymnast hasn’t played much in the way of shows yet, but here’s hoping they start touring, because this is much better than a lot of modern hardcore that’s just noise and incoherent screaming. ![Image 35](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/newagehealers-blowingsmoke.jpg) ## NEW AGE HEALERS – Blowing Smoke Through the Choir (newagehealers.bandcamp.com) New Age Healers is a Seattle band that defies the norm for the Pacific Northwest. Where most bands from that region tend toward heavy, gritty grunge and similar subgenres, New Age Healers dabble in a variety of other sounds, but focus on variations on shoegaze. In the past they’ve blended heavy sounds and psychedelia; on this LP, I hear a mix of shoegaze and indie pop. It’s lighter than past records, for the most part, and supremely pleasant. I love the opening track, “The Fastest Slow,” for that very reason. That’s not to say the band has completely given up psych or heavier sounds; those are here, too, but in smaller, more palatable doses. “Falling Apart” has some of both, to a degree. And “Ultra” really brings harder edgier sounds, but mixing in spacey vocoder style vocal treatments and guitar tone. The whole track has a hypnotic sort of style. “You’re the Sun” has some heaviness, too, with a hard driving low end and deliberate rhythm, and the song has a great melodic bounce, too. And “Devotion” blows the whole thing out of the water, eschewing the shoe-gaze aesthetic for a raucous post punk tune that’ll really get you jumping around. I really like the ethereal folk-pop sounds that are mixed into “Sunday Bed,” a song featuring guest vocals from Valerie Green. I am enjoying the evolution that band has displayed; the textures of these new songs are gorgeous and they’re varied enough to provide sonic stimulation and hold interest. That’s one thing that’s really tough to do with shoegaze, because sometimes the songs tend to all sound alike. Not so with _Blowing Smoke Through the Choir_, which I think is New Age Healers’ best album yet. ![Image 36](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/reserver.jpg) ## RESERVER – Reserver (Funambulist Recording Company) I’ve listened to this album about a dozen times over the course of a weekend and it’s left me dumbfounded. It’s the rare album that gets better and better on each subsequent listen, and this is one. It’s hard to describe the music, because there’s so much going on and yet it’s also so simple.Imagine combining the thick guitar noise of Jesus and Mary Chain with the melancholy of Joy Division, complete with baritone lead vocals. And the melancholy is real. Frontman Chad Preston stepped away from his previous band, The Laureates, when his wife Kerri was diagnosed with cancer. She sadly succumbed to her illness, but Preston got through those difficult years by writing songs, and with former Laureates bandmates Adam Penly and Crawfie Ward (guitar and bass, respectively) and drummer Dan Wendt, there was a drive to record those songs. As they say, they are a testament to the healing power of music. Right from the start, we’re in the thick of things. “Heart Is a Bomb” speaks to the inevitability of the loss of a loved one and the devastating impact that can have. I love the frantic guitar riffs and the somber bass lines, and the fatalism of the lyrics wrecked me (“Yesterday’s Papers uncovered the plot / Conclusion is coming, ready or not / The gods didn’t download your prayers or your thoughts / Sooner or later you’re here then you’re not.”) Another favorite is “Parallax,” a song that melds the sound of Joy Division with Mission of Burma’s style of song structure. Really, every one of the songs on this debut is a favorite, because they’re all so good. But it’s the mix of darkness and brightness of “Pyramids” that I think is the real stand-out. “I once said I wanna miss you / You know I do, you know I do / Someday I want to remember / You know I do / You know I do / I built this tomb to conceal you / It’s all for you, it’s all for you / You once said I won’t deceive you / I know you do, I know you do / But now you’re the sunshine.” The verses are the sad memories, but that one line chorus, “But now you’re the sunshine,” leaves me choked up. Music really does have healing properties. ![Image 37](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/ruckus.jpg) ## RUCKUS (Drunken Sailor Records, www.drunkensailorrecords.co.uk) When punk rock first emerged in the late 70's, it wasn’t fast and loud already. It began as a raw, simpler version of rock 'n' roll. And Boston’s Ruckus perfectly capture that loose feel, with power pop and good time rock and roll influences abounding. There’s a garage rock undercurrent, which fits perfectly with that early punk vibe, and you can just feel how much fun these guys are having playing the songs. Listening to the raucous music and the gritty throaty vocals on “Talk Ain’t Cheap Enuff,” you might forgive yourself for thinking you’ve falling through a time warp into a pub in 1978 London. Or listening to “Hot in the City,” you can feel the mix of influences of bands like The Jam and Ziggy Stardust era David Bowie. With Ruckus’ debut EP, they’ve recaptured the fun of rock and roll. * * * ![Image 38](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/gale%20forces.jpg) ## GALE FORCES – “Diviner” single (galeforces.bandcamp.com) A new standalone single from LA’s Gale Forces features heavy sounds with a Seattle influence, though the song also has the sound of 90's and 2000's alternative rock. There’s an emotional vibe to the song, which frontman Jade Devitt says was inspired by his partner challenging him to become more open and vulnerable in their relationship. He describes the experience as “frightening, but ultimately liberating.” The arrangement is already thick and lush, but I could imagine this being even better with strings and a less sludgy guitar tone. There’s a deliberate, slow pace to the song, pleading vocals, and an ending that’s unresolved. It’s an interesting listen. ![Image 39](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/kyeal.jpg) ## KYE ALFRED HILLIG – Widowmaker Express (kyealfredhillig.bandcamp.com) Imagine mixing Americana, folk, and moody indie-rock. The music is melancholy, with spare arrangements featuring guitars (acoustic and electric,) piano, drums, strings, and ethereal synths. This is the tenth LP from the Tacoma, Washington singer-songwriter Kye Alfred Hillig, and he says it was written in the wake of a health scare. He describes the album as a “breakup letter to the universe.” It’s an album, he says, that “wrestles with grief, faith, and the difficult work of carrying on.” The album is quite somber, with the hollow sound of reverb, Hillig’s vocals filled with uneasiness and anxiety. From the start, on “Oh Magic,” there’s a sense of loneliness and even despair. It starts with the gentle strumming of an acoustic guitar and Hillig’s singing, but some angelic backing vocals and piano join in subtly and delicately. And songs like “Coyote Skins” and “Fates Been Calling Through the Noise” feature otherworldly ambience set against soulful folk. There’s a bit of twang in some songs, courtesy of the lap steel guitar contributions of Graig Markel. And the strings on “The Ghost Will Turn Around” lend an almost spiritual quality to the song. But it might be “Indryd James” that steals the show here. The arrangement is incredibly delicate and understated, and the vocals convey a profound sense of loss. ![Image 40](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/iron%20filings.jpg) ## IRON LININGS – Urban Abyss (The Ghost Is Clear Records, theghostisclearrecords.com) Missouri’s Iron Linings formed in 2020, amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, and quickly recorded and released a debut EP to introduce themselves to the world. Following this was a split LP with Seaxes in 2022, and now comes their debut full-length. The band channels 90's post-hardcore noise blended with hard-hitting metal. The songs are frantic, filled with dissonance and unrelenting power. Rhythms constantly shift, vocals are shouted with intense ire, and unresolved tension fills every available moment of every song. As a result, each track, taken on its own, delivers an incendiary message, intended to spur movement and action. We get a mix of emo-core melodic lines, metallic riffs, and severely angular guitar jabs. The melodic friction generates fierce heat and catharsis. Taken together, the 12 tracks and more than 40 minutes of non-stop rage is overwhelming. Maybe too much. But I do like the riffs and interplay of the guitars and bass on “Red Mercury,” which has some moments that remind me of Circus Lupus. If you enjoy this sort of heavy hard-hitting metallic post-hardcore style, you’ll enjoy Iron Linings. ![Image 41](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/prisoner.jpg) ## PRISONER - Prisoner (Wicked Cool Records, www.wickedcoolrecords.com) What a ridiculously fun album! With 17 tracks and nearly an hour of music, you would think a couple of things: first, that the album is bloated and gets boring, and second, that this is a seasoned band that’s been around for a long time. You would be wrong on both counts. This is Prisoner’s debut LP, and it’s the furthest thing from boring you can get. They play an awesome mix of garage, synth pop, surf, and Stereolab-style psyche-pop, very atmospheric and very cinematic in style. Many of the songs remind me of 60's TV or movie soundtracks, especially those that had a Mod edge to them. And it’s either ironic or purposeful that the band’s name is “Prisoner,” because some of the music reminds me of the soundtrack to the short-lived but influential Patrick McGoohan TV show, _The Prisoner_. The album starts out with the high energy “La femme qui s’e´tait faite toute seule,” mixing retro psyche and garage, with instrumental music mixed with wild vocals in both French and English. It really sets a great tone for the album. I adore the breezy “Je ne retiendrai que toi,” with spoken vocals, muted trumpet, and a mysterious sound. “Borne pour obe´ir” is out of this world, with intense heavenly soprano operatic vocals and a cool Stereolab vibe, and “Il nous faudrait une bonne guerre” has a similar sound, though much more somber and melancholy. Some tracks are primarily instrumentals, some not. Many feature those intense operatic vocals. Many have horns, like “L’enfant qui est en moi parle,” which features trombone, and also synths tuned to sound like a harpsichord. It has a very dark mysterious sound, like the soundtrack to a 60s spy movie, but also has some great raucous garage rock moments. “Le paradis perdu,” or “Paradise Lost” is one of those instrumentals with operatic vocals, and the title is perfect because you can hear the loveliness of the paradise, but you can also hear the sadness and longing in the music. “Le village olympique” has a great psych-garage vitality about it, and the guitar tone and the trombone remind me again of “The Prisoner” TV show. Honestly, I can’t think of another band making music quite like this, and it’s just so much fun! They’re from France, and I sure hope they plan a US tour and come to San Diego, because I’ll buy a ticket to that! ![Image 42](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/rufio.jpg) ## RUFIO – From the Outside (Double Helix Records, doublehelixrecords.com) In the wake of major labels signing bands like Blink 182 and Sum 41 (which were, themselves, reactions to Green Day’s success), pop punk bands were in demand in the early 2000's. Enter Rufio, formed in 2000 in Southern California and named after the leader of the Lost Boys in the film _Hook_. Rufio were signed to Nitro Records in 2003, and released a couple of well-regarded albums. The mid-2000's brought tumultuous times for the band, with the departure of two members and their ultimate breakup. The following years saw sporadic reunion attempts, a “final farewell” show in 2007, and more shows in 2008 and 2009. Another new album followed in 2010, with plans for a world tour. And then the band called it quits yet again. One more reunion happened in 2015, and then… silence. But now, in 2026, the band decided to reissue an early hit, “Dipshit,” from their debut LP. And then they also announced brand new music, in the form of this five-song EP. And if you’re a fan of the sort of complex melodic pop punk of the 2000's, with simple poppy melodies and technical guitar work, you’ll love this EP. There’s skate-punk worthy speed on the title track and on “The Worst,” with intricate metallic riffs and super sweet pop melodies that would be right at home in a big arena. Other songs, like “Maps” or “Last Goodbye,” feature less speed and more slick production. They all feature those sugary strains. I have a lot of friends who will go wild for this. It’s a little too slick and commercial sounding for my tastes, though. ![Image 43](https://www.jerseybeat.com/Templates/images/cds/PaulSilver/sleights-allover.jpg) ## THE SLEIGHTS – Don’t Worry It Will All Be Over Soon (Rad Girlfriend Records, www.radgirlfriendrecords.com) Colorado Springs’ The Sleights are turning into quite a prolific band! Since last year’s spring release of their previous LP, _This One’s Gonna Hurt_, they released the "Atari" EP last fall and a split with Land of Wolves just a few months ago.
